Early parts deal with cost, fees, shops, and sales by bid. Later parts give tips on age, wear, fake aging, and care. Lewis sorts rugs by land and weave and shows key marks. Home buyers get firm rules they can use in a shop. Clear heads can spot a good rug and shun a poor one with his aid.
55500-twenty-drawings:
Twenty Drawings is a portfolio of art by Kahlil Gibran, issued by the Knopf house in New York in 1919. Alice Raphael wrote an introductory essay on Gibran's art. A plate called Towards the Infinite serves as the frontispiece. The twenty plates are listed by their titles at the front.

The Greater Self, The Blind, and The Mountain open the list of images. Flight, Centaur and Child, and Uplifted follow in the sequence. The Rock, The Waterfall, and The Burden carry the middle of the set. Great Longing, Veiled Face, and Crucified deepen the mystical tone. Compassion, The Struggle, and The Great Aloneness stand near the close. Mother and Child and a piece called Innermost end the twenty. Raphael presents Gibran as the leading artist and poet of modern Arabia.
55701-under-many-flags:
Under Many Flags is a book of missionary lives by Katharine Scherer Cronk and Elsie Singmaster. The Missionary Education Movement published it at New York in 1921. A front plate shows the American University of Beirut, with a note on mission schools and athletics. The book was made for study circles and young readers.

Eight lives carry the argument. Cyrus Hamlin of Turkey was a statesman and educator, and a baker by necessity. Hugh Tucker sold a million Bibles in Brazil. Barbrooke Grubb worked in Paraguay, Fred Hope in West Africa, and Mary Slessor in Nigeria, where she was called the White Queen of Okoyong. David Day served in Liberia and Jennie Crawford nursed in China. Each life shows a flag, a field, and a form of service.
57071-the-pursuit-of-happiness-a-book-of:
The Pursuit of Happiness is a book of studies by Daniel Brinton, printed at Philadelphia in 1893. McKay issued it, with copyright in 1892. Brinton also wrote Races and Peoples and The Myths of the New World. He inscribes the book to Justice George Pierce Andrews of New York, in memory of a friendship since their earliest college days.

The Declaration of Independence stands at the front, with its promise of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Whitman's lines on the drift of the stars follow. Part one asks whether a guide to happiness is possible, and whether happiness is a low and selfish aim. Brinton answers that we cannot do otherwise than pursue it.
5723-press-cuttings:
Bernard Shaw's Press Cuttings, dated 1913, is a short play set in the War Office on the morning of the first of April, 1911. General Mitchener sits at his writing table opening letters, while the machinery of government, press, and public opinion gathers around him. Shaw turns official business into comedy, letting generals, clerks, and journalists expose the gap between orders and sense.

The play's bite comes from its timing and talk: serious men handle absurd situations with perfect gravity, and Shaw lets their own words undo them. Readers and theatre groups will find a compact Shaw satire, easy to stage and sharp to quote. It suits those who enjoy political comedy that treats war offices and newspapers as twin stages for human folly.
57320-telescopic-work-for-starlight-even:
Telescopic Work for Starlight Evenings is a star lore book by William Denning. A Taylor and Francis house of London brought it out in eighteen ninety one. Denning once led the Liverpool star lore group in his past years. His front word tells how the book grew from sheet pieces of past years. Glass and glass work pieces ran in that group sheet in eighteen eighty seven.

More pieces on big and small glass and world watch went to star sheets. He cut, moved, and grew the whole till it stood near new in form. Some parts speak plain for plain folk, some hold facts for ham star men. Stanmore watch house stands in a front cut of the print in view. Uranus moon spans stand add to its lists from a late note there.
58086-roland-yorke-a-sequel-to-the-chann:
Roland Yorke is a novel by Mrs. Henry Wood, author of East Lynne, shown here in a tenth edition printed at London in 1880. It is a sequel to The Channings, and a verse from Longfellow stands at the front about a boy's will being the wind's will. A picture at the front shows a man shot in the leg.

The contents open with a prologue in the moonlight, then a death laid before the coroner, and the news carried home. Parts follow Roland through office life, unexpected meetings, and days of commotion at the firm of Greatorex and Greatorex. Later heads promise a private interview, a disappearance, and Roland Yorke's shoulder set to the wheel in earnest.
59176-selling-things:
Selling Things is a manual on salesmanship by Orison Swett Marden, printed at New York with copyright in 1916. Marden wrote Pushing to the Front and The Victorious Attitude. Joseph MacGrail, a teacher of salesmanship for large firms, helped him. The book is dedicated to Charles Schwab.

Twenty-nine chapters run from training the salesman to keeping fit. They treat the selling talk, the approach, tact, and sizing up the prospect. Later chapters cover closing the deal, meeting objections, and finding customers. An appendix adds sales pointers. Marden holds that character is capital, and that the man who can sell things is made, not born.
59380-building-with-logs:
Building with Logs is a how to sheet from the Forest Service of the farm board. Sheet five hundred seventy nine of its mixed set came out in September of nineteen forty five. Clyde Fickes, a works man, and Ellis Groben, chief house draughtsman, wrote it. Log build craft is plain once a few root rules are grasped, it opens. First folk past the east shore built of logs since boards were scarce.

An ax was their sole tool, so each good was hewn from wood by hand. Parts treat base work, log prep, and size choice in the first ranks. Round notch joints and other joint kinds get close how to parts. Wall lay, roof frame, chink fill, and hearth frame fill mid parts. Chair, bunk, chest, and board plans close the sheet with house plans.
59923-colorado-outings:
Colorado Outings is a railroad travel book by James Steele of the Burlington Route. The passenger department of the Burlington issued the guide at Chicago. The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad held the rights in 1898. A view of the Mount of the Holy Cross fronts the small book. Chapter one offers glimpses of a mountain world to the reader.

For thirty years no name had been writ oftener with height and vastness. Hundreds of books and millions of words had described Colorado's scenes. Yet the scenes themselves had never been described, Steele insists boldly. Colorado holds over a hundred thousand square miles in its bounds. Two-thirds of that vast area is mountains of the Titanic kind. Maps, details, and the camera must serve where words fall short. Time, distance, and routes fill the practical pages for travellers.
60046-tatlings:
Tatlings is a book of short wit lines by Sydney Tremayne. That name hides a woman who wrote for the press in her day. Drawings by an artist who signs as Fish dress the text. The book came out in New York in the year nineteen twenty two.

A gay front note pairs the two young gifts as a fit glove pair. Joy of life, wit, and keen sight of folk run through the small book. Each brief line aims for a neat sting or a bright twist of sense. The prints catch dress, pose, and mood of smart town life in the age. The whole forms a light gift book for fans of sharp brief verse.
60654-love-and-moondogs:
Richard McKenna wrote Love and Moondogs, a short tale first printed in Worlds of If in February 1959. A line at the start says the true dog came from the golden jackal. It adds that a dog must love and be loved, or it dies. That claim drives the whole tale.

News comes that a Russian dog has reached the moon alive and well. Four women in fur coats then haul a hound up a flag pole in a town square. Martha Stonery leads the group, which calls itself the United Dames of the Dog. They cry that chiefs are cowards and that the dog will starve alone in space. A crowd forms as the dog howls. McKenna turns a space race fear into sharp, sad farce.
61278-too-many-eggs:
Too Many Eggs, a science fiction story by Kris Melville, first appeared in Worlds of If for November 1962. Its transcriber's note records that no renewal of the magazine's copyright could be found. The tale is a piece of comic invention. Everybody likes fried eggs for breakfast, the opening asks, but would a chicken.

Coxe, a calm man hunting a bargain, buys a new refrigerator cheap because it carries a factory tag. It works perfectly, and he tests it by freezing ice cubes. Then packages begin to appear in the freezing compartment: fish eggs, which Coxe fries and finds very good. One package becomes two, then three, though nobody stocked them. His girl friend demands to know where they come from. Coxe is content to let the eggs keep coming.
61562-the-complete-collection-of-picture:
The Complete Collection of Pictures and Songs gathers the children's picture books of Randolph Caldecott. Routledge published it in London in 1887, in an edition of eight hundred copies. Edmund Evans engraved and printed the plates throughout. Austin Dobson supplied a preface on the artist and his work.

Sixteen short tales and rhymes fill the collection in their original dress. The House That Jack Built opens the set, as it opened his fame. The diverting history of John Gilpin rides in behind it. The Mad Dog and The Babes in the Wood follow in the first book's sequence. Three Jovial Huntsmen, Sing a Song for Sixpence, and The Queen of Hearts come next. Hey Diddle Diddle, Baby Bunting, and the wooing frog fill later pages. The Great Panjandrum closes the volume with a long final piece.
62444-the-preservation-of-the-exterior-o:
Paint specialists Allerton Cushman and Henry Gardner wrote this 1911 pamphlet for the Institute of Industrial Research in Washington. Cushman directed the institute, and Gardner led its division of paint work. The pamphlet takes up a plain question. What paint best protects and decorates the outside of wooden houses and other buildings?

The preface says the institute had studied building materials for years. Requests kept arriving for firm advice on which paints to choose. Long tests in many places let the authors give a definite opinion at last. They stress that no paint is attacked unfairly here. Each material is weighed for what it can do. The result is a buyer's guide to exterior paints, written by a research institute.
62665-classic-variations-in-cooking-with:
Classic Variations in Cooking with Texas Eggs is a state cookbook put out under Reagan V Brown, Commissioner of Agriculture for Texas. A front note asks if an egg is just an egg. The book flies the flag for food grown close to home.

Brown grants that the egg trade runs on the same health rules and grades in all states. Yet most Texans, he says, hold that home state food is better. A guide at the front sorts egg terms, from slightly beaten to stiff but not dry. It tells how to fold whites in and how to split an egg without breaking the yolk. Cold eggs split best, yet whites whip fullest at room warmth. Home cooks get clear egg craft plus Texas pride in one slim book.
62895-cartoons-by-mccutcheon-a-selection:
Cartoons by McCutcheon gathers one hundred drawings by John McCutcheon, printed at Chicago in 1904. McClurg issued it, and five editions passed between May 1903 and January 1904. The drawings first appeared in the Chicago Record-Herald. The famous Boy in Springtime series stands among them.

An opening essay praises two marks of his work. First, he draws public men without grossly insulting them. Second, he knows that politics does not fill the whole horizon of the American people. Older cartoons were savage caricatures tied to a paper's tariff views. McCutcheon's gentle humour and clever hand point another way. His pictures of everyday life, the essay says, are our real interest.
63270-deep-sea-plunderings:
Deep-Sea Plunderings is a book of sea tales by Frank Bullen. Appleton of New York brought the book out in March 1902. Bullen held the rights from 1901 and signed the preface at New Bedford. Eight illustrations stand through the gathered yarns of the sea. He gives the book to Doctor Robertson Nicoll in warm esteem.

Bullen had writ The Cruise of the Cachalot and The Log of a Sea-Waif. Through Fire and Water opens the contents of the tale set here. The Old House on the Hill, You Sing, and the Debt of the Whale follow. No apology for printing the tales in book form, he says flatly. Warned by past experience, he thanks his critics for their kindness instead. A four-masted clipper races for Melbourne in the opening tale told. She devours the degrees of longitude at some 360 miles a day.
6337-the-boy-allies-under-two-flags:
Boom, boom, speak the forward guns of the little scout cruiser H.M.S. Sylph, under Lord Hastings, as Jack in the pilot house cries a hit and Frank shouts good work to gunners who cannot hear him. A broadside follows, then German cruisers Breslau and Goeben answer from more than a mile away, shells throwing water in geysers round the little vessel like a typhoon. None finds its mark as the ships draw closer.

Ensign Robert L. Drake's Boy Allies tale follows Jack and Frank under two flags through Mediterranean fighting, with marksmanship as a test of nerve. Frank, challenged, fires twice at a knot on a tree, splintering it in midair with the second bullet, and tells a staggered midshipman he could have killed him with ease. The book is boys' war adventure, brisk, patriotic, and fond of guns, ships, and cool heads.
63636-the-glad-tidings:
The Glad Tidings is a study of the Epistle to the Galatians by Waggoner, published by the Pacific Press in 1900. Its chapters follow the letter: the real gospel, life by faith, redemption from the curse, the adoption of sons, the Spirit's power over the flesh, and the glory of the cross.

Waggoner argues that Galatians and Romans sparked the Reformation, whose watchword was that the just shall live by faith. That reform, he warns, is not yet complete, and its watchword needs sounding now as then. He refuses a scholarly introduction. The commentary that follows is written to send readers back to Scripture, verse by verse, rather than to rest in the commentator's opinions.
64016-a-paris-pair-their-day-s-doings:
A Paris Pair is a book of verse for the young by Beatrice Bradshaw Brown. Barbara Haven Brown made its plates. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty three. The book is sworn to a kin of the hand, named by marks a lone. Its verse walks a day in the life of two young folk of Paris, hour by hour. Each hour has its own short song and its own plate.

At eight of the clock the book starts. Jeanette is not a sleep head, the song says. It is an ease task to wake her. At eight she springs from bed, with no need to call or shake her. Her kin Jean is a more sad case, the song owns. His kind nurse is put to grief by his ways.
6429-many-ways-for-cooking-eggs:
Mrs. S. T. Rorer, author of Philadelphia cook books and Bread and Bread Making, gives many ways for cooking eggs, with sauces first. English drawn butter, plain hollandaise, anchovy, bechamel, tarragon, horseradish, cream, brown butter, Perigueux, tomato, paprika, curry, and Italian sauces open the book. Cooking of eggs follows, from preserving and egging and crumbing to shirred eggs, Mexicana, and eggs on a plate.

De Lesseps, Meyerbeer, a la Reine, au miroir, a la paysanne, and a la Trinidad join Rossini, baked in tomato sauce, and a la Suisse with nut brown butter. Birds' nests separate eggs, beat whites to stiff froth, heap them in dishes, make a hole, and drop in a whole yolk, then stand the dish in water and cover. Rorer writes a cook's catalogue, practical and generous, where one plain food becomes a hundred dishes.
64312-turner-s-sketches-and-drawings:
Turner's Sketches and Drawings is an art study by A J Finberg, published by Methuen of London, first in 1910 and here in a second edition of 1911. One hundred illustrations support the text. The frontispiece shows The Pass of Faïdo, a water colour of 1844.

Finberg calls sketches the raw material of art. The chapters follow the career in stages. Seven years of apprenticeship run from 1787 to 1793. The topographical draughtsman follows, then the sublime of 1797 to 1802. The sea painter of 1802 to 1809 comes next, with The Shipwreck beside the Death of Nelson. A chapter on simple nature covers 1808 to 1813. Finberg separates art criticism from aesthetic talk and names eight aspects of Turner's genius. The book taught readers to study drawings as seriously as finished pictures.
6459-the-girl-aviators-on-golden-wings:
Margaret Burnham's second Girl Aviators book opens on the great Nevada desert, white and glittering, dotted with gloomy clumps of sage brush. Peggy Prescott wrinkles her nose disdainfully at the view from the car window, and her brother Roy asks what she thinks of it. She will wait a while before answering, she says judicially, and Roy calls on Jimsy Bancroft, a lad his own age, with a slender, graceful girl beside him.

Jimsy laughs that there is plenty of desert anyhow, much like what he expected, and Peggy feels like a regular cowgirl already. A mid passage introduces an experienced plainsman who suggests lightening and adjusting their equipment, his odd manner of talking coming only at intervals. Peggy wonders if he acts a part, then doubts it as his gestures convince her otherwise. Burnham writes girls' flying adventure with desert, machines, and pluck.
65029-two-legs:
Carl Ewald wrote Two-Legs, a tale of man as the beasts see him, Englished from Danish by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. Frederick A Stokes issued the book in New York. Johan Briede and Helen Jacobs drew the pictures, some in full color. Four new chapters swell this form past the first.

The lead tale hunts for Truth lost from the world. Five wise men each bring back a unlike find. Then the beasts tell the life of Two-Legs in turn. A son is born, and Two-Legs learns to kill and to sow. Old beasts take counsel as his herds and fields spread. Wind, steam, and the electric force fall to him one by one. The close asks what his rule will mean for all life.
65067-it-s-raining-frogs:
Milton Lesser's It's Raining Frogs ran in Imagination in December 1950. An epigraph from Charles Fort's Lo opens it: we shall pick up an existence by its frogs. George sits on a beach under a cloudless sky while little red frogs rain on him. The fall is strictly local, a cone some fifteen feet across, and George is its center. Frogs strike his head, bounce off, and land on the sand. He runs toward the surf and the cone follows, the spot still over his head.

His wife Myra swims nearby, wrapped in a new idea of hers. When George shouts to her, the downpour thins to a drizzle and stops. Myra will be angry: left alone, the rain might have brought more than frogs. The headnote adds that a pretty girl falling into his arms would be another matter.
65327-cottage-cheese-recipe-book-appetiz:
The Borden Company made this Cottage Cheese Recipe Book, with parts from appetizers to desserts. Salads, salad dressings, breads, and main dishes stand between those ends. An opening note sets out the food value of cottage cheese in plain terms. One pound of it holds most of the protein, calcium, and iron of three quarts of milk. Three ounces give about half an adult's daily need of calcium, the book says.

Cottage cheese is a complete protein, easy to digest, the note holds. One ounce of the creamed kind gives about thirty calories, so it suits those who watch weight. It mixes well with almost any food, which makes it handy in the kitchen. Cooks get a full set of ways to serve one cheap, sound food.
65959-earth-s-gone-to-the-dogs:
William J McClellan wrote a tale first printed in Imagination in October 1954. Ruskin, head of Internal Security, rests at a farm on a bright spring day. His dog Daisy, soft haired and blue eyed, keeps him company on the porch. Tom the farmhand brings word that the digger Bigelow has come to call.

Bigelow begs that the dog be sent away before he will speak at all. He has dug near a crater where great pre-Atomic cities once stood. Fear of Daisy hints that dogs may not be what they seem. McClellan builds a sly tale from a calm porch and a wild claim.
6619-poems-and-songs:
Björnstjerne Björnson, the Norwegian poet, appears here in English verse kept in his own meters by Arthur Hubbell Palmer of Yale. Palmer's introduction notes a strange fact: a life of seventy-seven years yielded just two hundred pages of lyric verse, more than half written in about a dozen years. Yet what is true and strong, he says, finds room to grow without ink's aid.

The poems themselves mix thought, ire, and mirth, with a love of loud life's battles and a bard's pride in his nation. Palmer keeps the meters true, so the English sings like the Norwegian. Poems and Songs is a fine, short gateway to a Nobel poet's lyric heart.
66862-things:
Things is a book by Alice Duer Miller, published by Scribner in 1914. A series note lists the small gift book at fifty cents in boards. Miller had written The Blue Arch and Calderon Prisoner before this volume. Companion titles in the list run from Stevenson Christmas sermon to Van Dyke essays.

Slim, polished pieces for parlour reading were the Scribner gift book trade of the day. Miller wit, later famous in verse and fiction, works here in miniature. Such volumes were made for birthdays, prizes, and the bedside table of 1914. Readers gain a sample of a sharp American woman of letters in small form.
68972-sixteen-months-at-the-gold-digging:
Daniel B Woods wrote Sixteen Months at the Gold Diggings, a miner’s own journal. Harper and Brothers issued the book in New York in eighteen hundred fifty two. Gold found in far California had set the world in a roar. Tides of men set toward that one point from each land.

Woods worked the American and Tuolumne rivers and their side streams. Friends had begged him to keep a day book of the digger’s life. He rocked the cradle, swung pick and spade, and messed with miners. He knew the high of a strike and the low of a blank pan. Once, sick beneath a lone oak, he watched the stars to die. His notes show the road’s risks for the first bands of foot men. Young men in camps of vice get his grave warning. Gold tales for kin at home fill the plain, true pages.
69378-negro-workaday-songs:
Negro Workaday Songs is a book of the songs of work of the black folk of the South, by Howard Odum and Guy Johnson. Both men were of a great school of the south state. One held a chair of the lore of man in bands there. One was of a search house of that school. The book was put out in nineteen twenty six. It stands in a set of such study books of that school.

The set list at the front names the kin books of the work. The black man and his songs, the folk faiths of the south black man, and more study books stand in it. The sworn words of this book call its sing men a vast crowd. They are the glass of a race, those words say.
70274-inger-johanne-s-lively-doings:
A children's book translated from the Norwegian of Dikken Zwilgmeyer. Emilie Poulsson made the English version. Lothrop, Lee and Shepard published it at Boston in 1926. Florence Liley Young drew the illustrations. Inger Johanne is a parsonage girl in a small Norwegian town. Two earlier books told what happened to her.

The first chapter is addressed confidentially to readers. Inger Johanne laughs that she is an author herself now. Her earlier book was really printed, she marvels. Eighteen chapters of lively doings follow. A lost key, a dancing school, and a Midsummer bonfire appear. She nearly drowns once and surprises a clockmaker another time. A snow fight and a Christmas visit close the year. Zwilgmeyer's heroine became a classic of Norwegian childhood.
70360-a-cathcart-or-a-riggs:
Roy Norton wrote A Cathcart or a Riggs, a western tale of a mining town and a bold woman. Norton had told past tales of a made new reformer and of swords drawn for Spain. The blurb asks just who Pearl Brown is, so snappy and so bold. Two men make a bet on the point.

Pearl Brown had just laid out Patrick Sheedy with brass knuckles, the tale says. She had called Horace Ring, the reform chief of the Weekly Star, a chump to his face. She then caught the craze for reform that split the town of Murdock. Pearl bought the Alamo hall from the sheriff at a sale. Its row of thin sheds came with the buy. She gave its folk one hour at dusk to pack and clear out, and they did.
73227-the-nibelungs:
George Upton translated Ferdinand Schmidt's German retelling of the Nibelungs for young people, printed in Chicago in 1906. Four illustrations fill the book, one showing the death of Siegfried. It stands in a set of life stories for the young, beside Beethoven, William Tell, and Gudrun, at sixty cents a volume.

The translator's preface tells of the Nibelungen Lied, one of the world's greatest epics. It appeared in the twelfth or thirteenth century in south Germany, by an unknown hand. The poet used still older legends handed down by mouth. Historical and mythical elements mingle in the poem, Upton warns. It should not be confounded with Wagner's Ring, though the opera takes many names from the same hoard.
73597-the-three-strings:
The Three Strings is a mystery novel by Natalie Sumner Lincoln. Appleton published it in New York and London in 1918. Wrenn drew the illustrations. Lincoln had written several detective tales before it. A dedication challenges a friend to pull the right string. A chess expert helped work out a chess problem in the plot.

The first chapter is called The First Move. Evelyn Preston comes home to a closed Washington house. A September heat wave grips the city. She directs the taxi-driver with her luggage. Chapter titles promise complications and conflicting clues. A blotted page and a telegram advance the case. Bribery and identification follow near the end. The missing diagrams close the contents list.
7391-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Songs in Many Keys covers Holmes's middle years, 1849 to 1861, when he was lecturing, doctoring, and writing for every Boston occasion. The contents run from The Ploughman and Spring to songs after lectures on Wordsworth, Moore, Keats, and Shelley, and on to The Hudson and an ode for Washington's birthday. A farewell to James Russell Lowell and a Burns Club poem show his circle of friends.

The title fits: Holmes tries many keys here, from farmyard humor to civic ceremony. Beneath the occasional verse, the shadow of the coming Civil War gathers in poems about freedom and the Union. The volume is best read as a Boston poet's diary in verse, recording a dozen years of lectures, friendships, and public causes.
73936-the-price-of-eggs:
Randall Garrett's The Price of Eggs ran in Fantastic Science Fiction Stories in December 1959. Its note sets the stakes: royal babies are important on the planet Dynak, even though they hatch out of eggs. A mating arranged for one Boccaccio di Vino may cost him his breath.

Lieutenant Newhouse arrives on Dynak, sent by Sector Headquarters to solve a problem that has beaten the local commander, Colonel Hastings. The colonel receives him with stiff courtesy, praising his special training again and again, while making plain that book learning is no substitute for living with an alien planet. Garrett lets the interview run on the colonel's favourite word, appreciate, until the younger man's errand is clear. The tale is a dry comedy of rank, wounded pride, and alien custom.
7394-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
War dominates this volume, which gathers Holmes's songs of 1862 to 1874. Army Hymn, God Save the Flag, a hymn after the Emancipation Proclamation, and a puritan war song called To Canaan show a Boston poet rallying the Union cause. The Ballad of the Boston Tea-Party looks back to an earlier rebellion, while Dorothy Q, a family portrait, gives the war years a quiet, domestic counterpoint.

After the fighting come songs of welcome and farewell, union and liberty, and the flower of liberty itself. Holmes wrote many of these for public occasions, and they carry the plain, singable patriotism that made him a civic poet. The volume stands as a verse record of how the Civil War sounded in Boston parlors and meeting halls.
73942-the-madness-of-lancelot-biggs:
The Madness of Lancelot Biggs is a science fiction story by Nelson Bond, first printed in the magazine Fantastic Adventures in April 1940. Its headnote promises more than a football game at stake for Lancelot Biggs and the crew of the Saturn. Biggs, it says, traded his rocket emblem for a new uranium condenser, and it worked.

The narrator, the ship's Sparks, tells the tale. Just out from Lunar Three, his plates dull out under the audio bank, and Captain Hanson comes hunting the Space Manual. The captain's troubles, he sighs, would make the Sparks do cartwheels to Venus if they were as mild. Bond's recurring hero Biggs is a lanky, all-knowing engineer whose genius for pulling the Saturn out of tight spots is matched only by his gift for annoying her captain. The series mixes space opera with barracks humour.
74021-where-are-you-mr-biggs:
Where Are You, Mr Biggs, a science fiction story by Nelson S Bond, was first printed in Weird Tales in September 1941. The narrator is Sparks, radio man of the Saturn, an Earth-Mars lugger. At Mars Central spaceport a solar-gram orders the ship to Uranus at once to pick up a cargo of gallium.

Sparks calls Cap Hanson, who comes up from dinner scowling and bellows that the old crate cannot make the trip. The Saturn was built before the turn of the century and by all logic should have left the spaceways long ago. Only Cap Hanson and the screwball first mate, Lancelot Biggs, have kept her flying. Bond's tale is told in a salty, comic voice. It sets a tub of a ship and her odd crew on an absurd run to the outer planets.
74109-the-downfall-of-lancelot-biggs:
Nelson Bond wrote a gay space tale of Lancelot Biggs and his fall. The tale ran in Weird Tales in March 1941. Come aboard the Saturn for fun, the blurb cries in glee. Sparks, the wire man, tells the tale in his own voice. Three hours out of Long Island Spaceport, the fun starts.

Cap Hanson slips into the wire room with a red, round face. Shh, he hisses, with a fat thumb pressed to his lips. Is there anybody here, Sparks, he wheezes with care. Biggs, the ship's grand mind, stands at the tale's heart. Fads, tricks, and space-way jests fill Bond's romp. Light hearts rule it.
74138-the-love-song-of-lancelot-biggs:
Nelson S Bond wrote The Love Song of Lancelot Biggs, a comic space tale in Amazing Stories. The piece ran in the September nineteen hundred forty two issue. Sparks, the ship’s radio man, tells the tale in his own loose voice. His screwball pal, Lieutenant Lancelot Biggs, walks the bridge of the Saturn.

The Saturn hauls freight from world to world on plain runs. At Sun City port, a Mars clerk loads sealed lead casks in hush. Biggs stands by with his new bride Diane, lost in a sunset ode. All he wants is a ship board bouquet for his wife. The seeds he picks grow far too well, the head note warns. A dull haul to Uranus turns wild from that small want.
74173-the-return-of-lancelot-biggs:
The Return of Lancelot Biggs, a science fiction story by Nelson Bond, was printed in Amazing Stories in May 1942. Its narrator is Bert Donovan, radio man of the freighter Saturn, who calls himself the easiest going bug pounder ever to louse up the ether. At clearance time the radio turret door opens, and in waddles Cap Hanson with a grin from ear to ear.

Guess what, Sparks, the captain chortles: guess who just came aboard. Donovan groans at the thought of another know all like the encyclopedia on legs who hectored them from Luna. For Lancelot Biggs is back, the young genius who advises everyone. He tells the crew how to save juice by heating tubes before sending. He quotes facts and figures till the first mate grows haggard. Bond writes the series for laughs, in tall tale space slang.
74413-cape-cod-is-a-number-of-things:
Cape Cod Is a Number of Things is a book of sketches by Allan Neal, printed at the Register Press in Yarmouth Port in December 1954. The selections first appeared in a different form in the Soundside column of the Yarmouth Register. Neal writes as a man possessed by the Cape. A companion teases him that he talks of the place as if he owned all of it.

He admits the charge and sets out to answer her question: what is it between him and the Cape? His answer gives the book its title. Cape Cod, he begins, is a number of things and means a number of things. The sketches that follow test that claim against September afternoons of deep blues, green pines, and gleaming white sands. One piece follows car headlights in the half-light between yesterday and today.
74849-the-christmas-earnings:
The Christmas Earnings, or Ethel Fletcher's Temptation, by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, was published in New York in 1859. A Sunday school union issued the tale. A cover line gives its moral at once: if you want Christmas money, you must earn it. Ethel Fletcher walks home from school with her cousin Abby Coles. Christmas is near, and Abby has a shawl near done and scarfs to knit. Her father gave her five dollars, with five more promised.

Ethel has started nothing and hates to ask her father. He failed in business, and money is tight at home. Her mother was lately told to wait for new things. Abby treats failure lightly, since her own father failed too. The tale sets ease against want in a lesson for young readers.
74982-civil-service-jingles-and-other-th:
Civil Service Jingles and Other Things is a book of comic verse by Harry Walters. It was printed at Ottawa in 1911. The first piece is The Song of the Extra Clerk. Extra clerks call themselves fine knights of the pen. The permanent staff takes the credit, they sing. Extras do most of the work, the song claims. They are paid by the day and held as riff-raff.

Footnotes mock the verses as they go. One joke is dated to 1902 by its own note. A parable of Gastonio follows in prose. Gastonio fears his brother Alphonso has been discovered. Alphonso turns out to be a lobster of strong claw. Ottawa's government offices supply the whole scene. Clerks' grievances are turned to office humour here. The book is a small relic of civil service life.
75038-choice-sayings:
Robert C Chapman checked and shaped short notes on Bible texts for a new form. Morgan and Scott issued Choice Sayings in London from the office of The Christian. Heads run from The Gospel and Sin to Prayer, Love, and Praise. Each head holds brief, sharp lines meant for daily thought.

One line calls the first sigh over sin the start of an endless bond with God. More lines press trust in the blood of Jesus and warn the proud heart. Faith, church order, trials, and small things all get plain speech. Church readers of the time kept such books close for quick aid and calm.
76491-mary-russell-mitford-and-her-surro:
Mary Russell Mitford and Her Surroundings is a biography by Constance Hill, printed at London and New York by John Lane in 1920. Illustrations by Ellen Hill and reproductions of portraits fill the book. A portrait of 1836 fronts it. The binding's centre design copies a French gold enamelled watch that belonged to Mitford's mother and came down to the author of Our Village herself.

Thirty-nine chapters walk through the life in its places. An author's birthplace and happy memories open the book. The publication of Our Village stands at the centre, the sketches that made Mitford famous. Her play Rienzi, foreign neighbours, agreeable jaunts and eccentric neighbours fill the later chapters. Farewell to Three Mile Cross, Swallowfield, and peaceful closing years end the life. Hill writes a literary geography: the author known by the villages that surrounded her.
76584-lefty-o-the-blue-stockings:
Burt Standish wrote this baseball tale of Lefty and the Blue Stockings. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in New York in 1914. Past Lefty books took him to the bush and big league. A plate shows the horsehide humming into the outfield on a crack.

Contents open on an unlucky seventh and a stopped rally next. A summons from the manager, a girl, and theater scenes follow. Lefty stands in bad, grouchy, and on the raw edge early. A stranger, a retired manager, and a come back fill the late chapters. The game of his life and the girls in the box close the long contents list.
77634-peter-makes-good-and-stories-of-ot:
Gertrude Thomas's Peter Makes Good, and Stories of Other Dogs was published by Beckley-Cardy at Chicago in 1929, with twenty full-page illustrations by Dorothy Saunders. The title story follows Peter, a roly-poly, fuzzy, brown-and-white pup of mixed breeds. His father Shep and his Scotch collie mother Susie are worthy dogs, peaceable with the house cat. They train Pete in the Golden Rule for cats, and cuff him for stealing Betty's shoe, making him carry it back and wag an apology.

Five chapters take Peter to a new home and the farm. A second group, The Tattlers, tells of Pixie and Bob, Judge Airedale, Fritz who knew only German, Gyp the garbage man's dog, and the blind man's dog. The illustrations show Peter trying to put out a fire and helping bring the cattle from pasture. The book is school-market dog biography, moralised for young readers.
78120-the-marvellous-land-of-snergs:
The Marvellous Land of Snergs is a children's fantasy by Wyke Smith. Benn published it in London in 1927. Morrow drew the illustrations. Smith dedicated the book to his daughter Nina. Seventy-four short chapters divide into three parts. The Snergs are a small people living apart from the world.

The story begins at Watkyns Bay. Orphan children play in its waters each morning. Two of them, Sylvia and Joe, slip into the Snerg country. Gorbo the Snerg becomes their companion. A feast with the Snerg king follows. An ogre named Golithos dines with them later. A witch called Mother Meldrum keeps a house in the dark woods. Knights, castles, and a fearful bargain fill the later chapters.
78507-african-wanderings:
Ferdinand Werne wrote African Wanderings, an expedition from Sennaar to Taka, Basa, and Beni-Amer. J R Johnston translated it from the German, and Longman and partners published it at London in 1852. Werne had earlier written an expedition in search of the sources of the White Nile. The translator's preface grants that much has lately been done to explore Africa. No work, he says, surpasses Werne's Feldzug nach Taka.

None treats districts so little known, the preface adds. Blackwood's Magazine had called the German book curious in three ways. Werne wandered where no Christian, educated traveller had gone before. He campaigned as an officer in a wild, motley army, like a Moslem horde of the middle ages. And he lived long in camp, free to study tribes whose names few Europeans had heard.
79146-concerning-the-nature-of-things:
A popular science book by Sir William Bragg, published in 1925. Harper and Brothers issued it at New York and London. Many diagrams and plates illustrate the lectures. Atoms open the inquiry in chapter one. Gases and liquids follow in their turn. Crystals then take three chapters: diamond, ice and snow, and metals.

Bragg had won the Nobel Prize for X-ray crystallography. His Royal Institution Christmas lectures underlie this book. Alpha ray tracks and soap bubbles share its plates. The Cullinan diamond and Damascus blades appear among them. Camphor boats and oil on stormy water show surface forces. Bragg writes with a demonstrator's clarity and props. Generations met atomic science first through his lucidity.
79549-mrs-rule-s-foundlings:
Annette Lyster, who wrote A Leal, Light Heart and The White Gipsy, stands behind this tale for the young. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge printed Mrs Rule's Foundlings in London, with plates by Stacey. A front plate asks how old a found child might be.

Questions opens the tale, then Practical Answers. Armine's Trust and Making a Choice set the home in train. The first month, Mrs Anstruther's advice, and how it was followed fill the middle. The Baby, Fanny, Owen Morgan's visit, and Master Hastings name the young cast. Cast-off babes and the kind hands that rear them form the heart of this church press story.
79603-intellectual-things:
Intellectual Things, a book of poems by Stanley Kunitz, was published at Garden City in 1930 by Doubleday, Doran. Kunitz dedicates the book to Helen Pearce. Its title comes from a line of William Blake: for the tear is an intellectual thing. Some poems had already run in The Dial, Poetry, The Nation, The New Republic, and other journals of the day.

Near sixty short lyrics fill the volume, from Change and Geometry of Moods to Eagle, Benediction, and Promenade on Any Street. Titles like Rape of the Leaf, Prophecy on Lethe, and I Dreamed That I Was Old show the young poet's bent: thought pressed into image, love and death weighed in spare lines. The set marks an early, dense stage of a long career in American verse.
7982-a-traveller-in-little-things:
W. H. Hudson gathered these sketches from the New Statesman, the Saturday Review, the Nation, and the Cornhill Magazine into a book of small observations. Its contents wander from a Surrey village and a Wiltshire village to apple blossoms and a lost village. The vanishing curtsey, little girls he had met, Cromer beach, wild flowers, and a dog named Dandy. Fourteen of the pieces had already appeared in magazines.

Hudson's gift is attention: he finds a whole story in a gesture, a lane, or a childhood memory. The sketches read like walks taken slowly, with pauses for birds, people, and old customs. For readers who love English nature writing, the book is a gentle classic, and a reminder that the smallest things can hold a traveller longest.
7998-the-frogs:
Aristophanes, the great Athenian comic playwright, wrote The Frogs in the late fifth century BC, and it appears here in the Harvard Classics volume of nine Greek dramas. The play sends Dionysus, god of theatre, down to the underworld to bring back a great tragedian, since Athens has lost its best poets. There he judges a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides, with the fate of the city's art, and its spirit, at stake.

The comedy is bawdy, musical, and brilliantly parodic, mocking both poets while celebrating what theatre can do. Its chorus of frogs gives the play its name and its most famous joke. For readers new to Greek comedy, it is the friendliest starting point: funny on the surface, serious underneath, and still performed today.
8011-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
First Kings opens with David's death and Solomon's rise, then follows the building of the temple in Jerusalem, the king's wisdom and wealth, and his later drift into idolatry. After Solomon, the kingdom splits: Rehoboam keeps Judah, Jeroboam takes Israel, and a parade of kings follows, most of them faithless. Into this decline steps Elijah, whose contest with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel is the book's dramatic centre.

The history is told as moral account, with each king judged by faithfulness. Solomon's glory and Elijah's fire give the book its two poles: splendour and prophecy. In the King James Version, the temple building, the Queen of Sheba's visit, and Elijah's miracles remain among the Old Testament's most vivid passages.
8012-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
From Solomon's successors to the fall of Jerusalem, the second book of Kings tells the story of a divided kingdom. Israel in the north and Judah in the south drift toward idolatry and foreign alliances, warned by prophets Elijah and Elisha, whose miracles and confrontations fill the middle chapters. One kingdom after another falls: Israel to Assyria, and Judah, after a last reform under Josiah, to Babylon and exile.

The book reads as both history and judgment, explaining disaster as the fruit of unfaithfulness. Its vivid episodes, from Elijah on Carmel to the siege of Jerusalem, have entered common language. In the King James Version, the narrative's steady, sombre pace suits its theme: a people who had been given a land, losing it through their kings' choices.
8184-the-ghost-kings:
H. Rider Haggard's novel The Ghost Kings follows Rachel and Noie through a Zulu world of kings, omens, and spirits. Its chapters move from a girl and a boy, through goodbye and Ishmael, the casting of lots and the message of the king. To the taking of Noie, the omen of a star, a visit to the Inkosazana, Rachel's vision, and her loss and recovery of her spirit. Later chapters reach the mother of the trees, the city of the dead, the sanctuary, and a dream in the north.

Haggard writes adventure steeped in African legend, with Rachel as a white girl caught between two worlds and their spiritual powers. The novel's supernatural machinery, visions, curses, and ghost kings, drives its romance. For Haggard readers, it is a characteristic late romance, rich in atmosphere and in the author's fascination with Zulu belief.
8238-the-world-english-bible-web-1-kings:
First Kings, in the World English Bible, opens with David old and stricken in years, kept warm by the young Abishag the Shunammite, while Adonijah exalts himself, saying he will be king. The book, lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, follows Solomon's rise, the temple's building, his wisdom and later idolatry, the kingdom's split, and Elijah's stand against Baal. Its modern prose keeps the court intrigues vivid.

Readers meet a history told as moral account, where kings are judged by faithfulness. The World English Bible's plain style suits the narrative's pace, from palace plots to Carmel's fire. For those approaching Kings for the first time, this version offers the story without archaic language getting in the way.
8239-the-world-english-bible-web-2-kings:
Second Kings, in the World English Bible, opens with Moab rebelling after Ahab's death, and Ahaziah falling through a lattice in his upper chamber at Samaria. Sick, he sends messengers to inquire of Baal Zebub, god of Ekron, whether he will recover. But Yahweh's angel tells Elijah to meet them and ask why Israel seeks a god of Ekron when there is a God in Israel. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows Elijah and Elisha, the divided kingdoms, and exile.

The modern version keeps the prophets' miracles and the kings' failures vivid, from chariots of fire to the fall of Jerusalem. Second Kings here reads as a sombre history of a divided people losing its land. For readers of the histories, this rendering gives the story plainly, with its judgments intact.
8865-miss-theodosia-s-heartstrings:
Annie Hamilton Donnell writes Miss Theodosia's Heartstrings, illustrated by William Van Dresser, and dedicates it. A smile, to her husband, who could write so much better a book and dedicate it to her. Illustrations promise delicate fingers undoing the ravages of Stefana's patient endeavours, beautiful names except poor Elly, a girl asking to be put into a story like that. Evangeline establishing a stage of action outside the window. Chapter one opens with an exclamation: mercy gracious, answered by Miss Theodosia Baxter herself, a woman of few words.

The novel follows Theodosia, a New England spinster of strong feelings and stronger principles, through household, church. Neighbourhood life, where heartstrings are tugged by children, neighbours, and old romances. Donnell writes gently and humorously about a woman society might overlook.
9093-rural-tales-ballads-and-songs:
Robert Bloomfield published these rural tales, ballads, and songs in London in 1802, in the gap between The Farmer's Boy and its sequel. Written while his fame was fresh, the pieces treat village manners and country scenes, from a widow and her hour-glass to the Fakenham Ghost and the love of Walter and Jane. Bloomfield offers them on their moral merit.

The verse is plain, kind, and rooted in farm work, seasons, and parish life. Bloomfield, a working man himself, wrote from inside that world, not above it. The book keeps its charm as a record of English country life at the turn of the century, told in song.
9548-honore-de-balzac-his-life-and-writi:
Mary F. Sandars wrote Honoré de Balzac: His Life and Writings, first published in 1904, a life of the great French novelist. Sandars notes that little true life writing on Balzac then existed in English, though his fame stood high. Her book traces his complex mind, his debts, his toil, and his vast human comedy. She claims Balzac first gave plain men and women full weight in fiction.

Chapters follow Balzac from youth to fame, showing how he found drama in daily life, not in wild plots. His creed, drawn from Burns, holds that a man is a man for all that, rich or poor. A reader gets a clear, warm life of a giant novelist, and a guide to why his crowded world still draws readers today.
9809-the-price-of-things:
Elinor Glyn wrote The Price of Things in 1919, a novel of love, thought, and honeymoon discontent. Amaryllis Ardayre, on honeymoon in Paris at the Russian Embassy, hears a Russian claim that happiness needs banished thought. She puzzles at his words, having lived in the country as good as gold. Her husband Sir John seems dull beside school friend Elsie's promised thrills.

Glyn follows Amaryllis from Paris parties to a reckoning with desire, will, and the cost of probing life's meaning. Pandora's box opens as she thinks. A reader gets a frank, romantic Glyn novel, where a young wife learns what happiness truly prices.
9902-the-middle-of-things:
J. S. Fletcher's 1922 mystery opens with a man faced with reality, and a house at number seven in the square. Who was Ashton, and what do a ring and a knife mean? The early chapters send the searcher looking for a missing man, weighing speculations and secrets.

Later clues lead to a parish register, a visit to Paris, a grey mare inn, and a Japanese cabinet, as the middle of things slowly untangles. Fletcher, a prolific writer of detective tales, keeps the plot turning on small, concrete clues. Mystery readers get a neat puzzle in the classic British manner.
a-sappho-of-green-springs:
Bret Harte gathers four California tales, opening with the title story in the office of the Excelsior Magazine. A tall, dust-covered stranger with a long beard hesitates at the editor's door, carrying verses by a young woman of Green Springs whose poems have startled the magazine's readers. Who she is, and who speaks for her, drives the tale.

The Chatelaine of Burnt Ridge, Through the Santa Clara Wheat, and A Maecenas of the Pacific Slope complete the volume. Harte writes of editors, ranch families, and wheat country with his usual blend of sentiment and dry comedy. The title story plays gently with literary fame in a mining state.
a-traveller-in-little-things: William Henry Hudson gathers a traveller's sketches of little things in this volume. Fourteen first appeared in the New Statesman, the Saturday Review, the Nation, and the Cornhill Magazine. The contents run from how he found his title and an old man's delusion through stories of two brothers. Two white houses, a dog named Dandy, and a samphire gatherer follow. Surrey and Wiltshire villages, apple blossoms, freckles, Cromer beach, and a jackdaw complete the gathering.
anne-severn-and-the-fieldings: May Sinclair writes Anne Severn and the Fieldings, opening with children and following its heroine through the Fielding family world. The novel traces love, duty, and self-knowledge across years, in Sinclair's psychologically alert prose. It stands among her best studies of women's lives in early twentieth-century England. The close ties feeling to choice with care.
bab-ballads-and-savoy-songs:
W. S. Gilbert filled this volume with his Bab Ballads and songs from the Savoy operas, in a Philadelphia edition from Henry Altemus. The ballads began as comic verses for Fun magazine, signed Bab, and their nonsense carried Gilbert's fame before the operas did. Contents open with The Yarn of the Nancy Bell, Captain Reece, and The Bishop and the Busman.

Kings of Chickeraboo, the Bishop of Rum-ti-Foo, General John, and Sir Guy the Crusader march through the rhymes. A sample duet trades verses between He and She: a maid sickens for a gallant youth, neither can eat or sleep, and both ask what the poor soul should do. Gilbert's metre never stumbles, his rhymes snap shut, and cruelty and sentiment trade lines in perfect time.
britannica-1911-agricultural-gangs:
Agricultural Gangs were groups of women and children doing farm piece-work. An independent gang-master organized and supervised them. Farmers hired the gang for seasonal tasks. Public gangs differed from private gangs in employer. Private gangs worked for one farmer only. The system flourished in England's eastern counties. Cambridgeshire, Lincolnshire, and Norfolk were its strongholds. It survives modified in the fen district still.

Origins lie in drained marshland and poor-law quirks. Landlords avoided building cottages on reclaimed land. Parish poor rates fell on single parishes then. Cheap women and child labour filled the gap. Moral and physical ruin followed that nomadic life. Inquiry came with the child-labour commission of 1862. The Agricultural Gangs Act of 1867 set limits. No child under eight could be employed.
britannica-1911-allotments-and-small-hol:
Small plots for working men are weighed in a land entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An allotment is land split from a cottage and hired out. A labouring man works it to add to his main pay. A farm that feeds a man whole does not count here. Nor does the tiny yard plot that grows food for the house.

The heart of the fight is the labourer's share in land. Cash pay alone has never quite closed the farm bargain, men say. One shepherd drew just sixteen pounds of his sixty in cash. Grazing rights and crop ground on his master's land made the rest. That mix runs back to the manor world of old days. Thirteenth century farm books show the same two-class field world.
britannica-1911-bearings:
Bearings in engineering are the supports that carry a shaft load yet let the shaft spin free. A 1911 Britannica technical entry defines the pair as having one degree of turning freedom. The part of the shaft inside the bearing is commonly called the journal. Drawings show a small bearing block part by part for the reader.

The shaft is ringed by brasses made of gun metal or phosphor bronze metal. The lower brass sits in the main casting that forms the block base. Parts in the two drawings bear the same letters so each can be traced. The entry builds from that small block to the wider world of machine supports.
britannica-1911-bryan-william-jennings:
William Jennings Bryan (1860–) was an American political leader. This 1911 Britannica biography profiles his career. He was born at Salem, Illinois, on 19 March 1860. He graduated from Illinois College in 1881, as valedictorian. He took his law degree at Chicago in 1883. He practised at Jacksonville, then moved to Lincoln, Nebraska, in 1887.

Bryan sat in the House of Representatives from 1891 to 1895. He won notice by fighting protection. He also defended free silver at a ratio of 16 to 1. His “cross of gold” speech won him the Democratic nomination in 1896. The article follows his three runs for the presidency. He lost in 1896, in 1900, and again in 1908. It also covers his editorship of the Omaha World-Herald. Later he founded the weekly journal The Commoner. His stand against imperialism after the Spanish-American War also gets full treatment.
britannica-1911-cliff-dwellings:
Cliff-dwellings is the general archaeological term for the habitations of primitive peoples formed by using niches or caves in high cliffs. More or less excavation, or additions in masonry, shaped those homes in the rock. Two sorts are distinguished by archaeologists in the entry's scheme. The cliff-house is actually built on levels in the cliff, while the cavate house is dug out by using natural recesses or openings.

Great attention has gone to the North American cliff-dwellings, particularly among the canyons of the south-west in Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Colorado. Some of them are still used by Indians, the entry says. Modern research finds no definite justification for assigning them to a distinct primitive race, or farther back than the ancestors of the modern Pueblo Indians. Niches can be large, in cliffs a thousand feet high, approached by rock steps or log ladders.
britannica-1911-demetrius-macedonian-kin:
Demetrius is the name of two kings of Macedonia, and the article treats both reigns. Demetrius I (337-283 B.C.), surnamed Poliorcetes, the Besieger, was son of Antigonus Cyclops. Beaten by Ptolemy near Gaza at twenty-two, he freed Athens in 307 and was worshipped there as Soter, then destroyed Egypt's sea power in 306. His siege engines at Rhodes won him his surname though the city held out.

After Antigonus fell at Ipsus in 301, Demetrius took the Macedonian throne in 294 by murdering Cassander's son. Pyrrhus and his allies drove him out after six years, and he died a prisoner of Seleucus in 283. Demetrius II reigned from 239 to 229, fought the Aetolian and Achaean leagues, and died after a disastrous battle with the Dardanians.
britannica-1911-farm-buildings:
Farm buildings, the article advises, sit best facing south or south-south-east. A slight slope helps drainage away. Water supply comes first in planning: wells worked by engine, windmill or hydraulic ram. Water should be laid on at handy points, above all near stables and cow-sheds. The buildings belong near a public road, to save private road upkeep. They should also stand as near the farm's centre as can be managed.

On mixed farms of 200 to 500 acres, one rectangular block serves well. Stock-yards lie in the middle, parted by the cow-sheds. Cart-sheds, stables, stores and barn ring them round, with cattle-boxes and piggeries. Larger farms and dairy farms need their own arrangements. Local farming methods must shape the grouping in every case. The entry keeps to general principles and points readers to specialist manuals for plans.
britannica-1911-juangs:
The Juangs, or Patuas, literally leaf wearers, were a jungle tribe of Orissa, India, found only in the tributary states of Dhenkanal and Keonjhar. They numbered about 10,000 in all, and their language belongs to the Munda family. They claimed to be the first people of their land and denied any link with the Hos or the Santals.

They did not till the soil, but lived on game, snakes, and vermin. Their huts measured about six feet by eight, with very low doors. The boys of a village shared a hut that served as guest house and meeting place. The women had worn only girdles of leaves until recent times, a custom tied to a tale of the river goddess at the Gonasika rock. Their weapons were the bow and a cord sling. They held a vague faith in forest spirits and burned their dead.
britannica-1911-juba-kings:
Juba was the name of two kings of Numidia. Juba I, son and successor of Hiempsal, sided with Pompey in Rome's civil wars, from thanks for his father's restoration and from anger at Caesar. In 49 B.C. he crushed Caesar's army in Africa and killed its general Curio.

Drawn back to the Pompeian side, he shared the defeat at Thapsus. In despair he killed his companion Petreius and had a slave kill him, in 46 B.C. His son Juba II was carried to Rome as a child to grace Caesar's triumph. Well taught there, he received from Augustus the hand of Cleopatra Selene and his father's throne in 29 B.C. In 25 B.C. he was moved to Mauretania, with part of Gaetulia added. The date of his death is unsure, placed between A.D. 19 and 24.
britannica-1911-lodger-and-lodgings:
Lodger is a term of English law with more than one shade. In its strict sense it means one who takes furnished rooms in a house. The landlord lives in the house too and gives service. A looser sense covers bare rooms with no service. Boarders in a lodging house form a third case, set aside here.

Furnished rooms let for use at once carry a pledge in law. They must be fit to live in at the start. Break that pledge and the taker may walk away, owing no rent. No pledge runs that they stay fit. Bare rooms carry no such pledge at all. A lodger may use what the rooms need: bell, knocker, stair light. Rent seizure by a live-in landlord is a murky point. Most weight of view says no. All turns on true tenancy versus bare leave to stay.
britannica-1911-parry-sir-charles-hubert:
Charles Hubert Hastings Parry was an English composer born in the mid eighteen hundreds. The 1911 Britannica entry traces his schooling at Eton and at Oxford, where he took a music degree while still in his teens. He left a brief spell in business for art, and trained with several teachers at home and abroad.

The entry lists his early large works, from an overture and a piano concerto to choral scenes drawn from old verse. At first, trained hearers found his dense style hard to grasp. In time, songs and choral odes won him wide regard, and a famed eight part setting of Milton marked the start of a strong run of sacred and half sacred works.
britannica-1911-popham-sir-home-riggs:
Sir Home Riggs Popham is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a British admiral. He lived from 1762 to 1820. He was the son of Stephen Popham, consul at Tetuan. He was his mother's twenty first child at birth. He entered the navy in the year 1778. He served with the flag of Rodney till the war's end. In 1783 he was promoted to lieutenant in the service.

He was for a time engaged on survey work in Africa. Between 1787 and 1793 he had curious commercial adventures. Those adventures took place in the Eastern Sea. He sailed first for the Imperial Ostend Company. He then sailed in a vessel he had bought himself. He took several surveys in that time at sea. He rendered services to the East India Company as well. Those services were officially acknowledged by the company. But in 1793 his ship was seized by authority.
britannica-1911-ridings:
Ridings are the three districts into which Yorkshire has been divided since ancient times, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains the institution. The word was first written thrithing or thriding, but the opening th was swallowed by the th or t of the words north, south, east, and west that usually stood before it. Ridings are Scandinavian in origin.

In Iceland the third part of a county-like unit bore a kindred name, while in Norway the term marked a church division. A twelfth-century set of laws calls the riding the third part of a county. Cases that the wapentake court could not settle went up to the riding court. A case stuck there went on to the court of the shire. Charters of Henry the First name all three courts, and riding courts plainly sat after the Norman Conquest.
bully-and-bawly-no-tail-the-jumping-frog:
Howard R. Garis wrote bedtime tales of two frog brothers, Bully and Bawly No-Tail, for the Bed Time Series. A. L. Burt put out the book at New York. Louis Wisa drew the plates. The set's plan is plain on its own ads page: eight colour plates and tales for each day of a month, to be read aloud at night.

Garis's list of kin books runs long on the same page. Sammie and Susie Littletail head the animal line. Uncle Wiggily heads a line of his own. This book stands as number sixteen in the animal set. Frog ponds, jumps, and small scrapes form the stock a parent would find here. The No-Tail name gives the pair their mark at a glance. Short, soft tales for small ears are the whole aim, and the frog brothers carry it.
cabbages-and-kings:
O. Henry set this book of linked stories in Coralio, a port in the fictional republic of Anchuria on the Caribbean coast of Central America. The title comes from the Walrus and the Carpenter verses quoted at the front. A proem by the carpenter frames the tales, and the first story, Fox-in-the-Morning, starts the flight of a president.

President Miraflores flees his capital with the treasury funds and a singer, and the American adventurers of Coralio close in. Frank Goodwin, the banana magnate, and Billy Keogh, the cheerful photographer, run through the episodes. Lotus eating, forged telegrams, a suicide, and a hidden fortune braid the stories together. O. Henry wrote the book out of his own months in Honduras, and the banana republic he invented here entered the language.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-barl:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Barlings describes a Norbertine abbey about six miles east-north-east of Lincoln, founded in 1154 by Ralph de Haye and dedicated to Our Lady. Ralph gave lands to the Abbot of Newhouse, England's first Norbertine house, asking for a colony of White Canons at Barlings.

The abbey later moved to Oxeney in the same township, where Henry the Eighth dissolved it in 1537. Bishop Redman's register of visitations supplies much of what is known about Barlings and other English Norbertine houses. The register, kept in the Bodleian Library, covers some thirty-five years of visits and was published as Collectanea Anglo-Premonstratensia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthon-rafael:
Anton Raphael Mengs, Bohemian painter, born 1728, died 1779. He learned from his father Ismael, who moved to Rome in 1741. From his youth Mengs was energetic and skilful, appointed court painter before sixteen. He declined with modesty, returning to Rome to study.

He painted the Parnassus at the Villa Albani. He then went to Naples, executing a Caserta altar-piece, but quickly returned to Rome, then pressed into Charles III's service. He arrived at Madrid in 1761. Here he carried out many commissions, becoming St. Ferdinand Academy director. Once more he went back to Rome for his health. He returned to Madrid in 1773, painting the Apotheosis of Trajan for Charles III. Again his health broke down, and he returned to Rome. He died there, buried in San Michele church. His pastel and crayon works are among his finest. Many paintings are in Dresden and Vienna, with miniature portraits and Raphael copies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-konin:
Anthony Konings, born Helmond 1821, died 1884. After a brilliant humanities course he entered the seminary, conspicuous for piety. Feeling a monastic call, he entered the novitiate in 1842. His superiors sent him to higher studies. After teaching humanities, he was called onward.

His Moral Theology, Boston, 1874, based on Gury, won approval for simple language and succinct Alphonsus form. He first expounded the saint's views on equiprobabilism methodically. His American law knowledge enhanced his work's value. Later, at Bishop Mullen's suggestion, he published on episcopal faculties, revised and enlarged by Putzer. His pamphlet De Absolutione Parentibus was taken by the Holy Office as the basis of an Instruction to American bishops. Its very words entered the Third Baltimore Council Acts. Since then this Instruction has been the norm for absolving such parents. Konings was consulted across the United States, examined candidates, and served as an expert in ecclesiastical trials.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chronology-of:
An entry on the chronology of the kings of Judah and Israel, built first on a table of Bible data. For Judah the table gives each king, his age, length of reign, year of accession, and Bible reference, with s for son and b for brother of his predecessor. For Israel it gives length of reign, accession year, and reference, from Jeroboam the First through Hoshea.

The tables run from David, aged thirty with a forty-year reign, and Solomon through Asa and Josaphat. Israel's side runs from Nadab and Baasha through Ahab, Jehu, and Jeroboam the Second. The entry then weighs the figures against each other and against outside history, sorting reigns, co-regencies, and rival counts. It is a working tool for readers tracing the divided monarchy year by year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical buildings cover every structure raised for liturgical acts, whether called church, chapel, oratory, or basilica. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry treats the subject under history, division, erection, repair, consecration, immunity, and fabric. In the earliest days no buildings were set apart for Eucharistic worship, and assemblies met in private houses, as Acts and the epistles show.

Gatherings in the Temple, synagogues, or hired halls served teaching or prayer, not the Eucharist. By the end of the second century, dedicated buildings appear, and the entry follows their growth, upkeep, and legal standing. It closes with wardens, their election, and their duty to priest and bishop, plus the state law of church property in English-speaking lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-and-jo:
Edmund and John Jennings were brothers from Lichfield who both turned Catholic in hard times. Edmund, born in 1567, trained at Reims, was ordained in 1590, and came back to England under a false name. Seized while saying Mass in London in November 1591, he was put to death at Gray's Inn Fields that December.

His death changed his younger brother John, who at first had rejoiced to be rid of his pleading. John later wrote Edmund's life, joined the Franciscans, and rebuilt the English province of the order, dying at Douai in 1660. The entry moves from a short, brave mission to a long life of repair, and it is a vivid window on Catholic England under Elizabeth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeremiah-will:
Jeremiah Williams Cummings, an American priest and publicist born at Washington in 1814 and dead in New York in 1866. He was sent by Bishop Dubois to Rome's Propaganda College after his father's death moved the family to New York. Winning his doctorate, he returned as assistant at Saint Patrick's Cathedral.

Cummings proved a linguist, writer, musician, and popular preacher, and in 1848 Bishop Hughes set him to found Saint Stephen's parish. Intimate friend and disciple of Orestes Brownson, he managed Brownson's lectures and wrote often for his Review, sometimes more bluntly than Brownson himself. He also led priests and laymen resisting the Europeanising of the American Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-northmen-viki:
The Northmen, or Vikings, were Scandinavians who raided western Europe in the ninth and tenth centuries and then stayed as settlers. Tacitus already notes Baltic Suiones rich in ships, but the exodus proper began with small fleets off England and Scotland near the end of the eighth century.

Population growth, the breakdown of tribal order, and ambitious kings pushed Danes, Norwegians, and Swedes outward to Ireland, England, France, and beyond. The entry confines itself to that exodus, its causes, its fleets, and its slow turn from plunder to settlement. Tacitus already notes Baltic Suiones rich in arms, ships, and men.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-offerings:
Offerings, or oblations, are gifts presented to God in worship, distinct in this entry from bloody sacrifice. The word covers vegetable and lifeless gifts, and English Bibles use oblation, offering, gift, and sacrifice loosely for several Hebrew terms that lack sharp edges.

Found in every ancient Semitic religion, offerings are explained by tribute theory, by gift theory, and by communion theory, each weighed in turn. The entry then follows first-fruits, meal offerings, and incense through Israel's law into Christian usage and canon law. First-fruits offerings anchor the tribute theory, which sees the god as first owner of land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rings:
Rings in Christian use are surveyed here from New Testament times through the late Middle Ages. Christians, like others, wore rings according to rank, and Scripture mentions them without blame. Clement of Alexandria allowed a ring on the little finger bearing a dove, fish, or anchor. Tertullian, Cyprian, and the Apostolic Constitutions protested against showy display. The Acts of Perpetua and Felicitas tell how the martyr Saturus returned a soldier's ring as a keepsake.

Whether bishops wore rings early on is less certain. Augustine sealed letters with a ring, yet his biographer Possidius says he wore none, so a signet alone proves nothing about insignia. By 610, monks raised to bishop were described as wedded with the pontifical ring. The Fourth Council of Toledo in 633 ordered a restored bishop to receive stole, ring, and crosier. Isidore of Seville called the ring an emblem of pontifical dignity and of sealing secrets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-patrick-a:
Patrick Alfred Jennings, Australian statesman born at Newry, Ireland, in 1831, died in July 1897. Schooled in his native town, including engineering and surveying, he went to Victoria in 1852 and settled in the Saint Arnaud district, holding various public offices. Four years later he entered the Legislative Council, resigned in 1869, and won election to the Legislative Assembly.

Honored by Pius IX with the Order of Saint Gregory in 1874 and made a Knight Commander of the Order of Pius IX and Saint Gregory in 1876. He represented New South Wales at the Philadelphia Exhibition that year. Created Companion of Saint Michael and Saint George in 1879 and Knight Commander the next year, he served briefly as vice-president of the Executive Council in 1883 and colonial treasurer in 1885. In February 1886 he became premier and colonial treasurer, resigning in 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-richard-b:
Richard Bellings, Irish historian born near Dublin early in the 1600s, died in 1677. Son of Sir Henry Bellings, a Catholic landowner in Leinster, he trained in law at Lincoln's Inn, London. There he wrote a sixth book supplementing Sir Philip Sidney's Arcadia. Returning to Ireland, he entered Parliament and married a daughter of Viscount Mountgarret.

In 1642 Bellings joined the newly formed Irish Confederation, whose president was his father-in-law, and took the post of secretary to the Supreme Council. Sent to the continent in 1644 as the body's representative, he returned the next year. He worked as a royalist until 1649, when he withdrew to France, most of his property confiscated by Cromwellians. His chief work, a defense of Irish Catholics under the pen name Philopater Irenaeus, appeared at Paris in 1650. His account of Irish affairs from 1641 to 1648 was later recovered and published by John Gilbert.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-third-and-fou:
Hebrew Kings, split in Latin Bibles into Third and Fourth Books of Kings, are the history books expounded here. Hebrew Melakhim, or Kings, became in the Vulgate, following the Septuagint, Third and Fourth Kings, since they carry on First and Second Kings and close David's life begun there. Yet the work stands apart from Samuel, First and Second Kings, in origin, style, and purpose.

Division into two books at an awkward spot, mid-way through Ochozias's story, did not exist in early times and came later into Hebrew editions from Septuagint and Vulgate. Three parts fit the contents better. Part one, from First Kings chapter 1 verse 11, tells Solomon: God-given wisdom, temple and palace building, and splendour of his reign. Later parts follow Israel's divided kings to exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-votive-offeri:
Votive offerings are things vowed or dedicated to God or a saint and thereby set apart by consecration. The idea is very old, springing from humanity's instinctive attitude to higher powers seen as controlling the world by providence: to make a prayer more acceptable. The petitioner offers a gift, whether for the living or the dead, and the same impulse explains burying the dead with valued possessions.

In its more ordinary sense the practice means adorning shrines with objects of gratitude, on the theological principle of religion as part of justice, gift for gift. Votive offerings divide into things promised in trouble or crisis, and things presented in gratitude for recovery or deliverance without prior promise. They form an extremely varied list. Most commonly they represent the person favoured, the thing benefited, or the divine intervention itself.
daddy-long-legs:
Jean Webster wrote Daddy-Long-Legs, published in 1912, a novel told in letters. Jerusha Abbott is the oldest orphan at the John Grier Home. A rich trustee offers to send her to college. She has seen only his long shadow on a wall, with legs stretched like a daddy-long-legs spider. So that is the name she gives him. He requires her to write him a letter each month.

Signed Judy, her letters chart four years of study, friends, and first stories sold. They show a spirit growing bolder page by page. She does not know her backer's name, though he moves closer than she thinks. Webster's bright voice made the book a lasting favorite, and its mix of humor and grit still carries it.
divine-songs:
Songs for children, in words a child can sing, fill Isaac Watts's little book. Its full head says the songs were attempted in the easy language of children. A text from Matthew heads it: out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise. Watts inscribes the book to the three daughters of Sir Thomas Abney.

His letter tells how their parents housed him for two years of sickness at their country seat, with every comfort of life. The songs teach peace at home: birds in their little nests agree, and it is a shameful sight when children of one family fall out and fight. Hard names, he warns, may grow to clubs and swords. The Sluggard stands among the moral songs. The book taught generations of children their first hymns.
english-embroidered-bookbindings:
Cyril Davenport catalogues a lost luxury craft in English Embroidered Bookbindings, published in 1899 in the English Bookman's Library, edited by Alfred Pollard. Chapters sort the work by ground fabric: first canvas, then velvet, then satin. Dozens of plates show Bibles, psalters, and prayer books stitched with scripture scenes, symbols, and portraits.

The treasures include Queen Mary's Psalter, a fourteenth-century manuscript bound about 1553, and the Felbrigge Psalter. Princess Elizabeth's own handiwork appears twice: the Miroir of 1544 and Katherine Parr's Prayers of 1545. Davenport dates each binding and reasons from evidence like a missing coat of arms. The book preserves a courtly art that print and leather pushed aside.
far-off-things:
Machen's Far Off Things is a memoir of his youth in the eighteen-seventies and eighties. Arthur Machen published the book in London in 1922. He dedicates it to Alfred Turner, who saved the project from delay. The curtain had rung down on his youth, he writes.

Machen had held the book in his heart for many years. Looking back became his habit as he grew old. He recalls the far gone times when his life's scene was set. Without Turner, some day would have been never, he admits. Six chapters and a note make up the short volume. His other works listed include The Great God Pan and The Hill of Dreams. The memoir gives the mystic writer's own account of his beginnings.
fisherman-s-luck-and-some-other-uncertai:
Henry Van Dyke, minister, professor, and devoted angler, gathered Fisherman's Luck and Some Other Uncertain Things as essays on sport and life. He dedicates the basket of pieces to his Lady Graygown, warning there are no great fish in it, only little ones, shining pebbles, and wild flowers. Montaigne's remark that fortune shares even in certain arts supplies his text.
