Essays treat the thrilling moment, talkability, a wild strawberry, fishing in books, a Norwegian honeymoon, and who owns the mountains. Two named flies, a Bee-Pond and a Dragon, drift over a shoal in the practical passages. Van Dyke's gentle philosophy made the book a gift-volume favorite for outdoorsmen of his generation.
george-sand-some-aspects-of-her-life-and:
Rene Doumic, a French critic, wrote this study of George Sand, and the hosted text is the English translation by Alys Hallard, first published in 1910. Doumic says plainly that he offers not a full life but chapters on sides of it. His contents move from Aurore Dupin, the girl who became Sand, through the Baronne Dudevant, her married name, to A Feminist of 1832 and The Romantic Escapade.

Later chapters cover her loves and friendships, the humanitarian dream of her middle years, the revolution of 1848, and her late reign as the good lady of Nohant, her country house. A last chapter weighs the genius of the writer. Doumic writes with respect and some reserve about Sand's famous trousers, cigars, and loves with Musset and Chopin.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_CIA:
For years the CIA fought to keep its own internal history of the Bay of Pigs invasion secret. The agency argued that releasing the draft would confuse the public. Lauren Harper and Thomas Blanton compiled this briefing book, number 564, published in October 2016, when that fight ended.

A 2016 change in freedom of information law overturned the agency's stonewalling. The Archive's own lawsuit helped push Congress to add a twenty-five-year sunset on such withholdings. The record is thus two stories at once: a disputed invasion history, and a case study in prying documents loose.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Seventy-seven years after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, this Archive posting revisits one part of the record. Japanese reports at the time described radiation sickness among survivors. Leaders of the Manhattan Project dismissed those reports as propaganda.

Later science settled the question the officials had waved away: the sickness was real. Revisiting the dismissal matters because it was made by the men who built the bombs, about the people the bombs fell on. The posting preserves both the contemporary Japanese accounts and the American response, letting readers judge how evidence was treated when it contradicted a preferred story.

William Burr edited this briefing book, number 835, published in August 2023 for the seventy-eighth anniversary of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings. It reexplores the Manhattan Project record on radiation. Japanese reports of deaths and lingering sickness at the time confounded project leaders.

General Leslie Groves told the United States Senate that radiation sickness was a very pleasant way to die. A Navy report reached the opposite tone, calling the atomic bomb the most terrible agent of destruction known to man. Placing those voices side by side shows how the bomb's makers handled evidence of what their weapon did to human bodies.
hauntings:
Vernon Lee, the pen name of Violet Paget, wrote these four tales of haunts in 1890. Lee was a keen mind on art and the past, and she set her tales in Italy and England. The set bears the sub name Fantastic Stories, which fits its strange air.

'Oke of Okehurst' and 'A Wicked Voice' are the most known of the four. In one, a painter is drawn to a sitter who seems a ghost from a past age. In the next, a singer is cursed by a voice from the dead. Fine and cold, the tales are ghost craft as high art.
honore-de-balzac-his-life-and-writings:
Mary F Sandars published this life of Honoré de Balzac in 1904. Her first chapter owns the difficulty of a complete life of so complex a man. Little authentic word on Balzac existed in English, she notes. Yet the Realistic School then ruled fiction, and Balzac was its fountain.

Sandars praises Balzac for finding world interest in ordinary men and women. Common humanity, not sensation, was his ground, she argues. The man's courage and tenacity mark the political chapters. He would not stoop to evil doings even when his party urged it. English readers got a clear, admiring map of a giant's life and work.
hymns-and-spiritual-songs:
Isaac Watts wrote these hymns and spiritual songs in three books. The first book is collected from the Scriptures. The second is composed on divine subjects. The third is prepared for the Lord's Supper, the title page says.

The transcriber notes that reprints of Watts vary greatly. This file's first form came from an 1818 London printing. An index and a table of the Scriptures turned into verse close the volume. One hymn warns guilty ghosts of Adam's race to tremble and kiss the Son. Another marvels that the Eternal will dwell with us. Watts's hymns shaped English worship for two centuries and more.
indian-games-and-dances-with-native-song:
Alice C. Fletcher, holder of a fellowship at Harvard's Peabody Museum, arranged Indian Games and Dances with Native Songs in 1915. She dedicated the book to the youth of America. Her study came from sharing native life as far as she could, she writes. Finding Indian music in loneliness was like finding a hidden flower.

Part one gives a corn drama in five dances and an Omaha festival of joy. Hazard, guessing, and ball games fill part two. Movements match song in strict accord in the games she describes. Part three lists Indian names for camps and children.
kwaidan-stories-and-studies-of-strange-t:
Lafcadio Hearn's Kwaidan gathers Japanese stories and studies of strange things. Its title uses an older spelling of a word now said as kaidan. Hearn's many pauses and dots are part of his own style.

Tales include the story of Hoichi, a singer without ears. Others tell of a mirror and a bell, a dead secret, and creatures with long necks. Studies sit beside the tales, mixing folklore with reflection. The book remains a famous English doorway into Japan's ghost lore. Hearn retells these tales in calm, clear prose. The calm makes the strange events feel closer and more unsettling.
little-songs:
Eliza Lee Cabot Follen wrote these songs for little children. Cambridge published the first American edition in 1832. Follen hoped to catch Mother Goose's good-humored, musical nonsense. She presents the volume to little folks for their verdict.

A revised edition from Brookline, dated March 22, 1856, restores its name. Two captivating songs from an unknown hand join the collection. Above fifty pictures illustrate the rhymes throughout. Follen asks no praise beyond children lisping her songs happily. Two or three songs from the first edition return here. English editors had dropped them before Follen restored them.
love-songs:
Love Songs is a book of lyric poems by Sara Teasdale, the American poet. This text was copied from a 1918 reprinting of the 1917 edition. Teasdale, born in 1884, had already written Rivers to the Sea. The first poem remembers beauty, music, and an English lark, all for one beloved.

Poem after poem sings of love found, lost, and remembered. Her lines are clear, musical, and full of night, stars, and sea. The book won the first Pulitzer Prize for poetry. It made Teasdale one of America's best-loved poets of her time. Readers still turn to these songs for their tender honesty.
many-ways-for-cooking-eggs:
Many Ways for Cooking Eggs is a small cookbook by Mrs. S. T. Rorer. Rorer wrote the Philadelphia Cook Book and other valued manuals. Her contents begin with sauces, from hollandaise to curry. Then come pages of eggs in every dress a cook could wish.

Shirred, baked, steamed, and poached eggs appear in dozens of styles. Eggs come à la Reine, Rossini, Mexicana, and in timbales. Birds' nests, egg pudding, and eggs in tomato sauce vary the menu. Poached eggs alone arrive in some thirty named fashions. Rorer shows how one humble ingredient feeds a household richly. The book is a delight of early twentieth-century home cooking.
miss-theodosia-s-heartstrings:
Annie Hamilton Donnell wrote this sentimental novel, illustrated by William Van Dresser. Its heroine, Miss Theodosia Baxter, is a woman of very few words. The story opens with a child standing on her front porch, holding a still smaller child. Miss Theodosia's whole vocabulary for the shock is one word: Well!

Illustration captions name the children who invade her quiet life: Stefana, Elly, and Evangeline. Evangeline builds a stage of action outside the window. One caption quotes a wish to be put into a story like that. Donnell tells how an orderly spinster's heartstrings are pulled, one child at a time.
more-cricket-songs:
Norman Gale, schoolmaster and poet, published this second book of cricket verse in 1905. He dedicates it to a former pupil, John Denton, forgiving an old arithmetic lesson. The dedication poem toasts the lad with his useful fifteen and the bat who is lord of the green. Many songs first appeared in newspapers like the Westminster Gazette.

Titles celebrate every corner of the game: The Golden Game, The Dark Bowler, and The Old Professional. Doctor Cricket, Cricket and Cupid, and The Commentator widen the cast. Gale even thanks Prince Ranjitsinhji, the great Indian batsman, for reprint permission. His songs preserve village and school cricket as Edwardian England loved it.
more-tales-of-the-ridings:
F. W. Moorman, late professor of English language at Leeds University, wrote these Yorkshire tales. Elkin Mathews published them in London in 1920, after Moorman's death. He had edited a volume of Yorkshire dialect poems. The contents mix dialect stories with folklore: Melsh Dick, Two Letters, A Miracle, and Coals of Fire.

The opening tale treats Melsh Dick, a woodland spirit of the Pennines. His name means unripe, and he guards unripe nuts in the hazel shaws. Moorman traces his pedigree to satyrs and dryads of Greek myth. A grandmother's tales, including The Tree of Knowledge and Janet's Cove, preserve the Ridings' spoken traditions.
mr-scraggs:
Henry Wallace Phillips published these tales in 1906, told by his hero Red Saunders. The full title calls the book Mr. Scraggs Introduced by Red Saunders. Phillips had won readers with Red Saunders and Plain Mary Smith. Seven stories fill the contents list.

Titles promise proxy deals, sieges, and a fountain of youth. Picture captions hint at fights, jokes, and rough frontier talk. Scraggs is the odd friend at the heart of the fun. Saunders tells each yarn in a loose, comic voice. The book is Western humor of its day, full of tall talk and scrapes.
mrs-lirriper-s-lodgings:
Charles Dickens built this 1863 Christmas tale around a London landlady. Mrs. Lirriper keeps lodgings at Eighty-one Norfolk Street, Strand. She warns that letting rooms can rob a lone woman blind. One fine lady once stole her sugar tongs by a trick.

She tells all this as if talking to a dear friend. Her house sits between the City and St. James's. The parish rate books prove how long she has rented it. Through her eyes readers meet lodgers, debts, and small dramas. Dickens makes her gossip feel like love for the odd folk under her roof.
nasa-tm-19660024088-development-of-therm:
Conrad P. Mook of NASA's Space Vehicle Division gave this talk at a paint industry meeting in Dallas, Texas, in November 1964. His audience made paints and coatings for buildings and products. Mook came to explain a very different customer: spacecraft that must control their own temperature in orbit.

The talk describes NASA's research program on thermal control coatings. These coatings help a space vehicle absorb or shed heat from sunlight. Mook explains the special needs behind the program and how those needs were being met. The speech also shows NASA asking an ordinary industry to help solve an unusual space problem.
new-poems-and-variant-readings:
Robert Louis Stevenson's New Poems and Variant Readings appeared in London in 1918, long after his death. Chatto and Windus published the edition sampled here. Lloyd Osbourne wrote the preface, thanking the Bibliophile Society of Boston. That society had first found the poems and printed them for private readers.

Osbourne calls the poems full of self revelation, some painfully close and personal. The love poems, he says, vary in merit but share a touching sincerity. Stevenson kept them through all the moves of his wandering life. That care, Osbourne argues, shows he meant them to be published in the end. Prayer opens the contents list.
nonsense-songs:
Edward Lear's Nonsense Songs, Stories, Botany, and Alphabets pack his best known comic pieces into one book. The songs open with The Owl and the Pussy-Cat. The Duck and the Kangaroo, The Daddy Long-Legs and the Fly, and The Jumblies follow. The Nutcrackers and the Sugar-Tongs and Calico Pie keep the fun going.

Mr and Mrs Spikky Sparrow and The Table and the Chair round out the songs. Stories tell of four little children who went round the world. Seven families of Lake Pipple-Popple get a history of their own. Nonsense cookery, nonsense botany, and three nonsense alphabets finish the book. Lear's drawings go with the words.
nsa-watergate-six-things:
The National Security Archive, a research institute in Washington, published this briefing book in 2021 for the fiftieth anniversary season of Watergate. Luke A. Nichter assembled six findings from declassified Nixon White House tapes, memos, diaries, and FBI records. The documents are United States government records, open to all.

One item traces a call in which Charles Colson spoke of sticking it to Washington. Another follows the note by burglar James McCord that cracked the cover-up open. Each finding rests on primary documents printed with the briefing. The set shows how much of Watergate was still hiding in the files fifty years on.
oak-openings:
James Fenimore Cooper opens Oak Openings with a preface on wonder. Men live in the midst of marvels, he writes, without taking heed of them. A slight shift in political or social life excites discussion for months. Prodigies from above, shown daily, are received without surprise, as things of course.

Cooper argues that men dwell on interests they fancy they control. They neglect what plainly passes their understanding, he says. For himself, he believes the finger of Providence points the way for all races and nations. East and west alike travel a path so led, in his telling. The tale that follows grows on frontier ground under that creed.
pigs-is-pigs:
Ellis Parker Butler's comic story Pigs Is Pigs begins in the Westcote office of the Interurban Express Company. Agent Mike Flannery leans over the counter shaking his fist at Mr. Morehouse, and between them sits the whole cause of the fight: a soap box nailed into a cage holding two spotted guinea-pigs eating lettuce.

Morehouse points to the printed rates: pets, domestic, properly boxed, twenty-five cents each, fifty cents for two. Flannery finds the rule that an agent in doubt must charge the larger rate, and insists the animals are pigs at thirty cents each. The whole tale grows from that ten-cent quarrel over what a guinea-pig is, and it became Butler's best-known piece of humor.
podcast-tuckercarlson-dka2i27sxgs:
Tucker Carlson speaks in Australia as news breaks that Julian Assange is free. Carlson had long defended the WikiLeaks founder on air. The release ends years of prison and court fights.

Carlson hails the moment as a win for a free press. He recalls the charges Assange faced for publishing secret files. The crowd hears his reply live, far from Washington. He warns that the case still chills reporters everywhere. The episode preserves a host's instant reaction to a story he had covered, and championed, for years. Freedom, for one man, anchors the whole speech.
poems-and-songs:
Björnstjerne Björnson, Norway's great poet and dramatist, wrote the lyrics gathered in Poems and Songs. Rendered into English by Arthur Hubbell Palmer, a Yale professor of German, who kept the original metres. The American-Scandinavian Foundation published the translation in New York in 1915. Palmer's introduction presents Björnson as a lyric poet whose life overflowed his page: seventy-seven years of action produced only some two hundred pages of lyric verse.

Two poems quoted in the introduction state Björnson's creed: the poet does the prophet's deeds. The man who dares to stand in life's surge becomes his nation's best bard, whether he planned it or not. The songs themselves, many written in one intense dozen years, became part of Norway's national life, sung rather than merely read. English readers get the poet as his countrymen knew him, in singable translations.
press-cuttings:
Bernard Shaw wrote Press Cuttings in 1913, a one-act farce set in the War Office on the forenoon of the first of April, 1911. General Mitchener sits at his writing table opening letters, and starts convulsively at a voice outside crying votes for women. Snatching a revolver from a drawer before shame makes him put it back. His orderly reports another suffragette chained outside; the railings and everything chainable have been removed. The women have found the doorscraper, and she lies on the flags with her chain through it.

She claims the general holds the padlock key inside a letter in a buff envelope, and the envelope, impossibly, is on his table. Shaw built the comedy from militant suffrage against military pomposity, and Mitchener, a portrait of the brass hat at bay. Remains one of his neatest comic inventions: the empire's fist, frightened of a woman with a chain.
purple-springs:
Purple Springs is a novel by Nellie L. McClung, dated 1921, in twenty-five chapters with titles such as The House of Clay, The Power of Ink, The Doctor's Decision, and The Woman of Purple Springs. Its people live in a farming settlement where winter bites hard and small choices carry weight.

The book opens on the last day of February, an extra leap-year day of still, biting cold under lead-colored skies. Below John Watson's house the trees crack in the frost. The hens stay in. The pigs burrow into oat straw. The cattle crowd the big shed. Even the thick-coated dog Nap whimpers at the door.
rural-tales-ballads-and-songs:
Robert Bloomfield, author of The Farmer's Boy, wrote Rural Tales, Ballads, and Songs, printed in London in 1802 for Vernor and Hood and for Longman and Rees. In his preface Bloomfield says the poems were chiefly written in the gap of nearly two years between finishing and issuing The Farmer's Boy. Later pieces named there include The Widow to Her Hour-Glass, The Fakenham Ghost, and Walter and Jane. Friends read the poems before they were printed, and Bloomfield offers them with some trust in their moral merit.

Bloomfield writes frankly of what the fame of The Farmer's Boy did for him. He was not ready, he says, for the marked and, in his word, extraordinary notice the public showed that poem. It brought him many real blessings.
saunterings:
Charles Dudley Warner fills Saunterings with light travel sketches and opens by lowering every reader's hopes. Under the heading Misapprehensions Corrected, he jokes that the party will go somewhere yet learn nothing there. Such a book, he warns, could never serve as a school text or as study material for civil service tests.

Warner next recalls older Atlantic crossings, when travelers spent weeks at sea recording dull feelings in thick journals. Steamships now cross in eight or nine days and cables erase distance, so people think the ocean beaten. He insists its three thousand miles remain, rolling forties and all. A Boston salute of thirty-seven guns for Columbus lets him tease Italian pride and Spanish fame.
slavery-s-passed-away-and-other-songs:
Words by Edward Harrigan and music by Dave Braham give the title song of Slavery's Passed Away and Other Songs, under an 1887 copyright held by Wm. A. Pond and Co. The song was sung in Harrigan's drama Pete. An old speaker asks a child to sit by his knee and hear the tale of the bondage days before the war once more.

The verses recall rice fields and cane, the driver's whip, and mothers who lost their young. Chains and bloodhounds belong to the past in the song's telling. Freedom wears a crown, and the singer thanks the Lord and names Abra'm Lincoln for the change. Work still lies ahead, the last lines add, now that cruel slavery has passed away.
soldier-songs-and-love-songs: A. H. Laidlaw wrote Soldier Songs and Love Songs, under an 1898 copyright, printed at New York by the Press of William R. Jenkins. Laidlaw gives the book to the soldiers and sailors of the United States, whom he calls the two arms of American salvation. The contents open with Custer, The American Girl, and The Good Ship Ohio, then the Union Oath, Betsie Brown, Sword of Jehovah, and Black Eyes.
some-broken-twigs:
Clara M. Beede gives her poems in Some Broken Twigs, printed by the Press of Flozari, Pegasus Studios, at Cleveland in 1946. She gives the book to her granddaughter Betty Todd Bristow, the new mother. A list of her other books prints page-like numbers by their titles, among them Brown Plumes, More Brown Plumes, Sunshine and Rain, Clear Crystals, and Golden Leaves.

The first poem, To New York, calls the city a fairy land for maid and lad. Its bright lures draw the young, who take up life's test with true heart and hand on ambition's tour. Old trails, the verse says, are marked with scar and wand. Beede writes in short rhymed stanzas, and the Cleveland press shapes the book as a slim gift volume for kin and friends.
songs-of-the-ridings:
F. W. Moorman gives Songs of the Ridings to the Yorkshire members of the Workers' Educational Association. The contents name A Dalesman's Litany, Cambodunum, Telling the Bees, and The Two Lamplighters. Later poems treat Our Beck, Jenny Storm, The Hungry Forties, The Local Preacher, and The Flower of Wensleydale, with a preface at the front of the book.

Moorman's preface recalls a set of Yorkshire dialect poems he brought out about two years before. That book drew from many hands and spanned two hundred and fifty years, and it was well taken. Signs abound, he says, that care for dialect writing grows apace. His own songs here speak in that same broad Yorkshire voice, of dales, becks, chapels, and work.
studies-in-occultism-a-series-of-reprint:
Studies in Occultism No. 1 gathers three pieces by H. P. Blavatsky in the Point Loma edition of 1910, printed by the Aryan Theosophical Press at Point Loma, California. The series reprints Blavatsky's writings for students of theosophy, and a book list at the back points to its other numbers.

The contents are Practical Occultism and Occultism versus the Occult Arts, both from the journal Lucifer in April and May of 1888, and The Blessings of Publicity. Blavatsky draws a sharp line between true occult study, a strict path of training and self-rule, and the showy occult arts that chase powers and wonders. The pieces read as stern guidance for would-be pupils.
tales-of-the-ridings:
F. W. Moorman, late head of English at Leeds University, wrote Tales of the Ridings, issued in London in 1921 after his death. Moorman lived from 1872 to 1919 and also shaped a book of Yorkshire dialect poems. Five tales are listed, and a life of the author by Professor C. Vaughan opens the volume.

Vaughan traces Moorman to old Devon stock, born at Ashburton in 1872 where his father served as a church minister. He recalls a boy raised at the edge of Dartmoor who learned birds and flowers by heart. Readers meet both the man and his Yorkshire tales, with love of land and speech at the core of each.
tanakh-jps-1917-i-kings:
First Kings is a history book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the 1917 English Bible of the Jewish Publication Society. It takes up the royal story where the books of Samuel leave it, with King David old and worn near death.

David lies cold in bed despite heaps of clothes, so a fair young woman, Abishag the Shunammite, is brought to care for him. Meanwhile his son Adonijah lifts himself up as king, with Joab and Abiathar at his side. Nathan, Zadok, and David's mighty men hold back. Readers enter a court split over who will rule next, setting up Solomon's reign, the temple, and the long line of kings that follows.
tanakh-jps-1917-ii-kings:
Second Kings is a history book of the Hebrew Bible, presented in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society English version. It opens after the death of Ahab, when Moab breaks away from Israel's rule.

King Ahaziah falls through a lattice in his upper room at Samaria and lies sick in bed. He sends men to ask Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, if he will live, but Elijah meets them on the road. The prophet asks why a king of Israel would seek a foreign god at all, and sends back a word of death. Readers follow the last kings of two split realms, with prophets, wars, and falls of cities leading toward exile.
tanakh-jps-1917-song-of-songs:
Song of Songs is a book of love verse in the Hebrew Bible, here in the Masoretic-based English of the Jewish Publication Society, 1917. It is headed as the song of songs, which is Solomon's, the finest of songs.

A woman longs for her beloved's kisses, saying his love tops wine and his name pours out like scented oil. She calls herself black but lovely, darkened by the sun while tending others' vines. The two trade praise, seek each other, and meet in gardens and fields. Readers get bold, lush love poetry, long read both as human love song and as a figure of God's love for his people.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-11-1-k:
First Kings in the King James Version begins with an old King David who cannot get warmth from clothes laid on him. Servants propose finding a young virgin to stand before him, cherish him, and keep him warm.

A fair damsel, Abishag of Shunem, is found across Israel and brought to the king, whom she serves. Then Adonijah, son of Haggith, exalts himself and says he will be king. He prepares chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him, and confers with Joab and Abiathar. An unchecked son and a dying king set a succession struggle in motion.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-12-2-k:
Second Kings in the King James text, starts with Ahaziah, king in Samaria, sick after falling through a lattice in his upper chamber. He sends messengers to enquire of Baalzebub, god of Ekron, whether he will recover.

An angel sends Elijah the Tishbite to meet those messengers. Is there no God in Israel, Elijah asks, that they go to Ekron? The word returned is stark: the king will not come down from his bed, but will surely die. Messengers turn back with that report. Prophetic rebuke and a foreign god frame a book of failing kings.
the-boy-allies-under-two-flags:
Ensign Robert L. Drake wrote The Boy Allies Under Two Flags. The first chapter is called In the Mediterranean. It opens in the midst of a sea fight. The two front guns of the small scout cruiser H.M.S. Sylph speak at once. Jack, in the pilot house, cries that the shot was a hit, and Frank shouts praise the gunners cannot hear.

The Sylph swings and pours a full side of fire into the foe. Then guns answer from more than a mile off. The German cruisers Breslau and Goeben are firing back. Shells fall on all sides and throw up great spouts of sea, and shells scream past her tops. None strikes home. As the ships close, a British shell lands true and tears part of the Breslau's upper works away. A cheer rolls over the Sylph, and Jack is called to the bridge.
the-claverings: An editorial note, rather than any chapter text, is all that is present for this novel. The note records that the story first ran in The Cornhill Magazine from February 1866 to May 1867, then appeared in book form from Smith, Elder and Co. in 1867. It also records sixteen full-page illustrations and sixteen vignettes by Mary Ellen Edwards, a respected illustrator, and explains which sets each edition carried. The author's name is not stated in what is given, so the plot cannot be summed up from this material.
the-fall-of-the-nibelungs:
Margaret Armour turned the old German epic of the Nibelungs into English prose as The Fall of the Nibelungs. Thirty-nine adventures fill two books, from the first news of Siegfried to the last deaths in Etzel's hall.

Siegfried comes to Worms, wins Kriemhild, and helps Gunther win Brunhild. Then the queens quarrel, Hagen plots, and Siegfried is betrayed and slain. The hoard comes to Worms, and Kriemhild's grief turns to a long plan of revenge. Her marriage to King Etzel draws the Burgundians east, where hall, fire, and sword end the line of kings.
the-frogs:
Aristophanes wrote The Frogs, a comedy of old Athens, shown the year after the death of Euripides. An introduction in this Harvard Classics copy sums the poet's life and art.

Aristophanes was born in Athens in the fifth century B.C. and had his first play staged while still so young his name was kept back. Over forty plays are credited to him; eleven stand whole. His satire strikes at politics, faith, and letters with bold jests born of the Dionysus feasts. In The Frogs the god Dionysus goes down to the dead to fetch back a poet fit to save the city.
the-ghost-kings:
H. Rider Haggard wrote The Ghost Kings as a tale of Zululand, in twenty-four chapters from The Girl and The Boy to The End and the Beginning. A letter dated 1855 opens the tale.

The letter tells a strange Zulu tale of a white girl in Dingaan's day who held the spirit of a white goddess of legend. Her title was Lady of the Zulus, and she was the child of a wandering missionary. Dingaan killed her parents, she went mad, and her curse was blamed for his death and the Zulu defeats. Haggard builds his romance on that seed: Rachel Dove, a missionary's daughter, taken for the goddess reborn.
the-girl-aviators-on-golden-wings:
Margaret Burnham wrote The Girl Aviators on Golden Wings. It is marked as No. 2 of a series. Chapter I is called The Great Alkali. It opens on a train crossing the Nevada desert. Peggy Prescott looks out at the white, glaring waste. She sees sage brush here and there. She holds back her verdict on the place.

Her brother Roy teases their friends. Jimsy and Jess Bancroft join them in the car. Jess says she feels like a cowgirl already. Peggy mocks her for guarding her skin with cold cream. The light talk sets up a young crew of fliers. They are headed west, keen for flight and new sights in a hard, dry land.
the-lullaby-with-original-engravings:
The Lullaby, printed in New London by John R. Bolles with original engravings, is a small book of poems for children. Its Evening Song watches twilight fall: dew on the roses, birds in the nest, a lamb resting on the green. The singer asks the child to rest while silent stars shine and angels keep their watch of love. She prays that the Saviour who was born a child will guard the baby night and morning. A second poem, The Robins, follows two robins building a nest of sticks, straws, and feathers in an apple bough among blossoms.

Four little birds lie hidden under green leaves, peeping and flapping while the old ones feed them. The verses are gentle and pictorial, pairing bedtime prayer with simple nature observation for very young readers.
the-middle-of-things: J. S. Fletcher published the mystery novel The Middle of Things in 1922. Only the contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The chapter titles open with Faced with Reality and Number Seven in the Square, then ask Who Was Ashton? Later chapters promise a ring and a knife, speculations, and a parish register. The closing run brings a Japanese cabinet, an Ellingham motto, a claimant, and the demand 'Let Him Appear!'
the-old-bush-songs: A. B. Paterson, author of The Man from Snowy River, edited The Old Bush Songs, printed in Sydney in 1906, songs composed and sung in Australia's bushranging, digging, and overlanding days. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the song texts themselves do not appear. The contents list Two Aboriginal Songs, The Old Bullock Dray, Bold Jack Donahoo, The Wild Colonial Boy, John Gilbert (Bushranger), and On the Road to Gundagai.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol: Songs in Many Keys (1849 to 1861) form this section of The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes in the 1893 three-volume set. Here only the section title and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. Titles include Prologue, Agnes, The Ploughman, and The Study. The Bells, Non-Resistance, The Moral Bully, and The Mind's Diet appear too. Several pieces mark lectures, including poems after lectures on Wordsworth, Moore, Keats, and Shelley. Occasional verse names a farewell to Lowell, a Washington's birthday ode, and The Living Temple.

Songs of Many Seasons (1862 to 1874) form this section of Holmes's Poetical Works. A bracketed note calls the file Volume 2 of the 1893 set. Here only the section title and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The contents group poems as In the Quiet Days, with Dorothy Q and The Organ-Blower. In War Time brings God Save the Flag! and a hymn after the Emancipation Proclamation. Songs of Welcome and Farewell name a farewell to Agassiz and a dinner to Admiral Farragut.
the-price-of-things:
Elinor Glyn's novel The Price of Things, dated 1919, opens in Paris during a honeymoon. A Russian guest lays down a rule for happiness: banish all thought, since probing the meaning of things opens Pandora's box. Amaryllis Ardayre, a bride at a party at the Russian Embassy, asks in puzzlement how one can not think. Until now she has accepted things without speculating about them.

The narrator weighs the two men before her. Sir John, her husband, is a fine figure of an Englishman, but dull. One can be certain he will always do his duty. The Russian is huge, ugly, and rough-hewn, with yellowish-green slanted eyes. Yet he is plainly a personality, with unknown possibilities tucked away. He studies the charming English bride in return, full of temperament and commonsense, and reflects that educating her would be an agreeable task.
the-sea-fogs:
Robert Louis Stevenson's The Sea Fogs carries an introduction by Thomas Rutherford Bacon. The book is Western Classics number one. An epigraph from Longfellow pictures cold mist climbing a castle wall. Bacon begins with Stevenson's first California trip. Stevenson came in 1879 for the purpose of getting married, he writes.

Delays to that marriage are set forth in Stevenson's letters and life, Bacon says. The last obstacle was the breakdown of his health. In connection with that attack, Stevenson first mentioned the sea fogs. They beset much of the California coast. Bacon calls them poisonous to anyone with pulmonary weakness. To others they are bracing and glorious, he says. Stevenson's courage and determination to be happy won him fourteen more fruitful years, in Bacon's account.
the-story-of-sigurd-the-volsung-and-the-: William Morris's epic poem of Sigurd the Volsung and the fall of the Niblungs appears here in an eighth impression issued by Longmans, Green, and Company in 1904. Only the title page and a contents opening appear here. The list sums up book one. It names King Volsung's dwelling and his daughter Signy's wedding. The fall of Volsung and his sons follows. The birth of Sinfiotli and King Sigmund's death close the heads. The poem itself does not appear. A companion record carries a condensed school edition.
the-wild-tribes-of-davao-district-mindan: Fay-Cooper Cole's Wild Tribes of Davao District, Mindanao appeared in 1913 as a Field Museum ethnology publication in the R. F. Cummings Philippine expedition series. The pages present here give the title page and table headings, so Cole's ethnography does not appear. Headings show a foreword by Charles B. Cory and sections on the study area's location and extent, its natural geography, and its inhabitants' physical characteristics. Table titles name the Mangguangan place-name meanings and the Manila hemp trade.
the-world-english-bible-web-1-kings:
First Kings, book eleven of the World English Bible, begins with an aged King David. Servants cover him with clothes, yet he cannot get warm. They search Israel for a beautiful young woman to care for him. Abishag the Shunammite is brought to the palace. She cherishes the king and serves him.

Meanwhile Adonijah, David's son, declares himself king. He gathers chariots, horsemen, and fifty runners. Joab and the priest Abiathar back his claim. David had never once challenged the young man's behavior. A succession struggle thus opens the book. Readers follow how Solomon's throne is secured amid court intrigue.
the-world-english-bible-web-2-kings:
Second Kings, book twelve of the World English Bible, starts after King Ahab's death. Moab rebels against Israel in the vacuum. King Ahaziah falls through a lattice in Samaria and lies sick. He sends messengers to consult Baal Zebub, god of Ekron. Elijah the Tishbite intercepts them with a rebuke. Is there no God in Israel, the prophet asks.

The sentence is stark: Ahaziah will not leave his bed alive. The messengers return and report the hairy prophet's words. Prophecy and kingship collide throughout this book. Readers watch two kingdoms slide toward exile. Elijah and Elisha stand as stubborn witnesses against royal idolatry.
true-riches-or-wealth-without-wings:
T. S. Arthur's True Riches; or, Wealth without Wings was published at Boston in 1852. His introduction explains a change of title. He first chose Riches without Wings, then learned that a similar volume existed and a new edition was coming.

Arthur argues that real wealth must be stored in the heart. Gold, the god of this world, cannot bless anyone who lacks that inner wealth. His story dresses the lesson for young and old alike, with all the winning attractions he can give it. Parents concerned for their children's best interests are his named audience. The tale that follows teaches through household incident rather than sermon.
uncle-remus-his-songs-and-his-sayings:
Joel Chandler Harris addresses the new edition of Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings to illustrator Arthur Barbette Frost. Fifteen years after his first book, Harris writes, the public has dealt gently and generously with Uncle Remus. The new edition brings new type, new pictures, and new binding to unchanged matter.

Harris confesses himself at a loss for a preface word. He pictures thousands of children's faces, young and aged, and hears one voice say, You have made some of us happy. Letters from children and from adults who stayed children at heart fill his memory. Fifteen years, he muses, is old age for a book, yet some green sap runs under the gray bark.
under-two-flags: Ouida, the pen name of Louise de la Ramee, wrote Under Two Flags, a story of a soldier's life dated 1867. She dedicated it to Colonel Poulett Cameron, whose family sent many soldiers to the armies of France and England. The pages here give the dedication and a contents list of numbered chapters without titles, and no story text is shown. Readers learn from the dedication alone that the tale honors soldiers and takes army life as its subject.
unhappy-far-off-things:
Lord Dunsany published Unhappy Far-Off Things in 1919, a book of short pieces shaped by the recent war. It opens with a sonnet, A Dirge of Victory. The poem asks Victory to blow her trumpet not over troops, but over hollows full of old wire. There the long dead lie among rusted iron. The poem insists that the dead earned the wreath more than the living did. They waited through hundreds of nights for her coming.

A prose piece on Arras Cathedral follows. Dunsany finds the great steps crowded with a silent procession of young trees. Some stand in green and some have turned yellow. Men and women no longer worship there, so the trees have come with wind and rain to take their places. Readers get brief, strange, sad sketches. They turn ruined places into quiet fables about loss.
watersprings: Arthur Christopher Benson wrote Watersprings, dated 1913. Pages present here hold the title page and a contents list of thirty-two chapters, so the novel itself is not shown. The chapters sketch a quiet plot. They name the scene, restlessness, and a place called Windlow. A pool, the home circle, and the vicar follow. A stay with Maud alone, a boy named Jack and his escapade, and diplomacy come next. The new knowledge, the new life, and a return to Cambridge close the list.
wells-brothers-the-young-cattle-kings:
Andy Adams published Wells Brothers, subtitled The Young Cattle Kings, in 1911. The novel follows two young brothers who start with almost nothing on the western plains. Their story is set against cattle drives, ranch work, and hard winters.

The contents list twenty-two chapters with names about claiming a range, holding a fort, and finding water. Chapter one opens in the summer of 1885 with a herd leaving Dodge City, Kansas. A drover named Don Lovell owns the herd, and one of his men is hurt on the trail. Readers get a plain, close look at cowboy work and risk.
whirligigs:
O. Henry gathered twenty-four short tales in Whirligigs. The set includes his famed piece The Ransom of Red Chief. The first tale, The World and the Door, opens with a jab at writers who claim a tale is true. Truth, they say, is stranger than fiction, and O. Henry sets out to puncture that claim.

His yarn, he says, came from a Spanish purser who swore by a shrine that a vice-consul told him the facts. That official, O. Henry notes, could not have known half of them. A policeman's flat line in a made-up tale beats real life for strangeness, he jokes. Sharp twists and warm humor fill the set.
